info.title: Museum Flack
info.subtitle: A Practical Public Relations Guide for Museums

personblurb.para: Steve Lott is corporate communications executive with more than 20 years of experience developing strategic public relations strategies and brand campaigns across diverse industries including aerospace, manufacturing, transportation, consumer brands and international trade policy. He is also professor of strategic communication at American University, where he teaches a graduate- level university course about media relations.

Representing more than 35,000 individual museum professionals and volunteers, institutions, and corporate partners serving the museum field, the Alliance stands for the broad scope of the museum community.
The American Alliance of Museums’ mission is to champion museums and nurture excellence in partnership with its members and allies.
Books published by AAM further the Alliance’s mission to make standards and best practices for the broad museum community widely available.

abstract.para: A simple review of recent news media coverage about museums and institutional leadership shows that the field is facing public scrutiny never seen before in its history. Museums are under a microscope and their leaders are ill-equipped to handle the unexpected (and often negative) media attention. At the same time, museum executives have little experience and training when it comes to public relations (PR) and their institutions are often too small to employ a communications expert. The effect of this ’perfect PR storm’ includes missed opportunities to positively promote museums in the news, as well as some bungled PR responses that have led to tremendous reputational damage. There are many books in the museum field focused on different aspects of marketing focused on a variety of topics including increasing membership, raising contributions or attracting new audiences. But a search for a practical guide on museum public relations and strategic communications turns up very little – three books in the past 40 years. Many museums have little help or resources to help understand the news media, social media or crisis communications. A simple how-to guide is long overdue and needed now more than ever. Steve Lott, corporate communications executive and former journalist, is an experienced storyteller who provides real-world public relations strategies and media training. In Museum Flack, Lott shares his own experience developing and executing successful media campaigns from the world of aerospace and technology, as well as case studies and lessons learned from the museum field. Museum Flack is a how-to guide that gives insider tips, tactics and tools to get positive media coverage, as well as strategies to deal with crisis communications. An effective media relations strategy requires very little budget but does require planning that can ultimately deliver positive, national news coverage or save a museum’s reputation. The target audience for Museum Flack is for museum professionals who are interested in learning about public relations and strategic communications. The book is written for a wide audience that ranges from students to museum directors and board members. This how-to guide will include museum-specific case studies and examples that will be relevant for students who are just entering the museum field to professionals who have spent their whole career in the field but have little experience dealing with the news media.

dedication.para: To my wife and daughter, whose unwavering support illuminates every page of this journey.
To my parents, whose legacy as exceptional communicators taught me the true essence of sharing ideas.
To my students, whose inquisitive minds remind me of the transformative power of communication.
This book is dedicated to all of you, and to the power of communication and understanding as cornerstones of society.

preface.para: Today, museums and cultural organizations find themselves navigating challenging and complex communications and public relations issues. This is no surprise as the essence of a museum is to collect and interpret the past and present to help better inform the future. By default, and mission, museums will always find themselves at the center of contemporary discourse, headlines, and politically charged issues.

Why are they collecting an object? What stories, individuals, and narratives are museums highlighting? How should a museum revisit history? These questions are central to helping the public better understand the consequential work museums do every day. So, how can museum leaders be better prepared to address these questions and drive the narratives of our organizations? How do you create winning public relations strategies that better address these questions, and how do you manage crises when they arise?

Over the last few years, I have had the opportunity to visit Professor Steve Lott’s classes at American University to discuss the media landscape and global and strategic communications. One of the items we always stress to students when navigating complex stories for corporations, not-for-profits, and associations is the need to anticipate the unexpected when it comes to public and media relations.

Many museums have small teams, limited budgets, and constant demands, so it is challenging to spend time preparing for the unknown. Some small museums have one or two communications professionals charged with all aspects of communications, from internal to external, social media, web content, media relations, and crisis communications. However, as Professor Lott outlines, being prepared with a few basics, no matter how small your organization, can help you successfully land the stories and pitches you want and can help you navigate the not-so-good stories. When facing so many constraints, preparation for the unexpected is key to a successful PR and media strategy.

section.para: Newsrooms and reporters have limited time and resources. Gone are the days of a team being assigned to a story. Today, across different media outlets, a reporter must be multi-talented; he or she must write, research, edit, and develop content for different platforms in different ways.

Whether it is an on-air interview, written story, social media post, or a podcast, reporters have pressing deadlines, changing demands, and short turnaround periods. For stories, reporters need relationships with museum professionals they can trust and that understand the changing media landscape.
How do you build trust with a reporter and get your story or narrative across?

listitem.para: Facts matter. Words matter.
Relevancy is key.
Get to the point.

section.para: The key to building trust with a reporter is confirming and providing facts and offering additional or helpful context when a reporter is writing a story. We might have pitches and stories we want to land, but first, we must become a trusted and credible resource to an editor or reporter.
So many of us have received a dreaded call or email from a reporter that starts with, “I’m hearing… about your organization/principal/exhibit/… and I think it’s interesting… so I am writing a story.”
Your immediate response must always be: “How can I be helpful?”
Followed by: “Please send your questions my way and I will track down the answers (facts!) for you.”

For every story, whether you are on the receiving or pitching end, preparing a rundown of the key facts you want to see in your story is paramount. You might know all the details off the top of your head, but writing a rundown will force you to create a cadence and question some assumptions. After you have the facts (who, what, where, and how), it is not enough to know what happened; you need to outline the why. Why did this happen? Why is this important?

Some professionals confirm, deny, or provide the who, what, where, and how but do not strategically outline the why. In finding out the why, you discover new facts. What was the impetus, the catalyst, and the need? Why did the museum choose this object, this story, that person? This is part of the story that the reporter may not know; initial facts do not reveal the totality of a story. The why is your story. When preparing for a story, time and again, it is important to continue to ask why.

The only thing more important than the facts is the words we use to describe the facts. A single word or phrase can change the direction of a story or become the story. Two things can be true at the same time, but strategic framing and articulating can change perceptions, understandings, and opinions. In this digital world, when organizations are seeking headlines that lead to clicks and followers, it’s important to always remember that words matter.

When pitching or working on a developing story, our words should be intentional, nuanced, and exacting. The power of language and the words we use should communicate meaning, convey feelings, and illustrate stories. After establishing facts, it is the words we choose that will inspire, deject, anger, drive, move, and potentially propel us to have a more complete understanding.

Every day, reporters get countless pitches. When I worked in television, I had a drawer full of pitches, stories, tapes (back then!), and ideas for stories and programs. I called it my personal black hole. Nowadays, email provides an effortless way to pitch a story without being too intrusive. However, how do you ensure your pitch does not go into a digital black hole? Relevancy and timing are key.

When pitching a story, always ask yourself: How is this story relevant to this moment? How is this exhibit telling stories that need to be told today? Why does this story matter to the reporter’s audience? What is the urgency of this story? It is essential that you know the audience, or you will waste everyone’s time and discredit yourself. If you do not have answers to these questions, you should not be pitching the story.

Most reporters are interested in new stories. They are hungry for stories that are compelling, fresh, accurate, relevant, and, if appropriate, exclusive. However, like museum professionals, reporters have daily deadlines, pressures, and limited time. Reporters appreciate pros that can succinctly and accurately get to the point.

Anyone who has ever worked with me has heard me say: Give me the headline. What is the main point? Think back to how we learned to write our first communications. First, an introductory paragraph, then the first paragraph with the main sentence, followed by the supporting sentences and a conclusion. Always remember you need a main sentence (a headline) for every paragraph, pitch, and story before the story is written. Give the reporter your headline when pitching a story so that he or she can understand the essence and direction of the story.
Get to the point quickly and efficiently.

A museum’s charge includes inspiration, exploration, discovery, and learning from the individual to the global level. Telling the stories of history, culture, science, and art while contextualizing the present-day can deepen audiences’ understanding of what came before, as well as help them envision the future and have a better understanding of society and the world around us.

Museum and communications professionals are central to amplifying these stories with expertise in delivery. We serve as a vital bridge between a museum’s mission and the public. We can shape public education, perception, and opinion by bringing the museum’s exhibits, collections, and programs to new audiences. In this book, you will learn how our work can inspire, raise awareness, and foster understanding that promotes, protects, and raises the profiles of museums and cultural organizations.Museums are vaults brimming with world treasures, and museum professionals have the privilege and responsibility of unlocking the vaults and bringing them to life for new and vast audiences.

listitem.para: Like other any industry or field of study, public relations (PR) and media relations have their own terminology
Understanding the words and jargon at the beginning of this book will help with the reader’s understanding of the concepts and strategy.
This terminology guide has a mix of PR, marketing, and advertising words.
Media relations is the ongoing facilitation and coordination of communication and relationships between an individual, group, or organization, and the media.
Like all PR, media relations is built on relationships and trust.

info.title: Introduction to PR Terms and Jargon

section.para: PR is a dynamic and multifaceted field that encompasses a wide range of activities, strategies, and communication techniques. As with any specialized profession, PR has its own set of terms and jargon that practitioners use to describe their work and navigate the complexities of the industry. Understanding these terms is essential for anyone involved in PR, whether you are a seasoned professional, a newcomer to the field, or a stakeholder seeking to collaborate with PR experts.

public relations terms and jargonkey termsThis directory of PR terms and jargon is designed to serve as a comprehensive reference guide, providing clear and concise definitions of key concepts, practices, and tools used in the PR industry. From foundational terms like “press release” and “media relations” to more advanced concepts such as “crisis communication” and “thought leadership,” this glossary covers the breadth of PR terminology.

The purpose of this guide is to demystify the language of PR, making it accessible and understandable for all. By familiarizing yourself with these terms, you will gain a deeper insight into the strategies and tactics employed by PR professionals to build and maintain relationships with the media, manage reputations, and communicate effectively with diverse audiences.

Whether you are preparing for a PR campaign, collaborating with a PR agency, or simply seeking to enhance your knowledge of the field, this glossary will be an invaluable resource. It will help you navigate the intricacies of PR, enabling you to communicate more effectively and make informed decisions in your PR endeavors.

The reader should explore this glossary and discover the rich vocabulary that defines the world of PR. As the PR industry continues to evolve, staying informed about the latest terms and trends will empower you to stay ahead and achieve your communication goals.

glossdef.para: The act of arguing on behalf of a particular issue, idea, or person.
The specific group of people that PR efforts are directed toward, which can include customers, stakeholders, employees, and the general public.
The degree to which a brand is recognized by potential customers and correctly associated with a particular product or service.
The creation and sharing of online material (such as videos, blogs, and social media posts) that does not explicitly promote a brand but is intended to stimulate interest in its products or services.
The process by which an organization deals with major unexpected events that threaten to harm the organization, its stakeholders, or the general public.
Statistical data relating to the population and particular groups within it, which is often used to identify target audiences.
Publicity gained through promotional efforts other than advertising, as opposed to paid media, which refers to publicity gained through advertising.
A schedule used by publishers, businesses, and PR professionals to control publication of content across different media, including blogs, newspapers, magazines, and social media platforms.
The interaction between people and brands on social networks and involves likes, comments, shares, and so on.
A type of movement or campaign that starts at a local or lower level, relying on support from the average citizen through direct and personal involvement.
A person with the ability to influence potential buyers of a product or service by promoting or recommending the items on social media.
The practice of using a variety of communication disciplines (advertising, PR, branding, digital marketing, etc.) in a coordinated manner to reinforce each other.
Using something to maximum advantage, such as leveraging media coverage to enhance one’s business objectives.

The ongoing facilitation and coordination of communication and relationships between an individual, group, or organization, and the media. This includes managing and building relationships with journalists and broadcasters to communicate a client’s newsworthy messages, stories, and information.
Any media content that you control and is unique to your brand, like your company’s website, blog, or social media channels.

glossentry.glossterm: public relations terms and jargonmedia relations terminologyPaid Media:

glossdef.para: Any media that is paid for and you control the content. Examples include traditional advertising or a sponsored or paid article or video interview.
How a brand or organization is perceived in the minds of a target market relative to its competitors.
A specialized area of PR that builds and maintains governmental and local community relations in order to influence public policy.
The practice of shaping the public perception of a person or organization by influencing online information about that entity.
A performance measure used to evaluate the efficiency or profitability of an investment; in PR, it often relates to the impact of communications on business outcomes.
A short, fast-paced video that gives the audience a feeling for what’s being presented, using highlights and big moments.
A person, group, or organization that has an interest or concern in an organization.
A particular group of consumers identified as the recipients of an advertising or PR campaign.
Content generated by an organization’s experts that provides insight and perspective on industry trends or key issues, positioning them as industry leaders.
A factor that differentiates a product or service from its competitors, such as the lowest cost, the highest quality, or the first-ever product of its kind.
A marketing technique that uses social networks to produce increases in brand awareness or to achieve other marketing objectives through self-replicating viral processes.
The specific emphasis chosen for a story that determines the approach and perspective from which the story will be covered.
An informational document often provided to the media along with a press release to give deeper insights into the context, statistics, and details about the subject matter.
The specific subject, sector, or industry that a journalist routinely covers, such as the technology beat, the healthcare beat, and so on.
A communication technique used in interviews to transition from the interviewer’s question to a specific message that the interviewee wants to communicate.
Supplemental or alternate footage intercut with the main shot in an interview or broadcast news story.
The line in an article that names the author of the piece.
A selected portion of a piece of media content (such as audio or video) used to demonstrate or highlight a particular point or to report on what has been broadcast or published.
The line at the beginning of a news article that includes the date and place where the story originated.
An agreement between sources and journalists that information provided in advance will not be published until a specific date and time.
A news story that is given to only one newspaper or broadcaster, potentially giving it an advantage over competitors.
A concise document providing key information on a new product, event, or other subjects, often formatted as a series of bullet points to allow for quick understanding.
A type of non-news article that provides an in-depth look at a particular topic, trend, person, or organization, often highlighting personal stories and experiences.
Highlighting or drawing attention to a particular part of a press release or media pitch, usually to signal its importance or relevance.
A subsequent action where a PR professional contacts a journalist after sending a press release or pitch to ensure it was received and to gauge interest.
An individual who controls access to something, especially information or exposure in the media. Examples include a news editor or producer.
A compelling angle or piece of information that grabs the attention of journalists and their audiences.
A core idea conveyed by an individual or organization to their target audiences, including the media, shareholders, the public, and other stakeholders.
The opening paragraph of a press release or news story that summarizes the most important points. It should include the Five Ws (who, what, when, where, why).
A brief notice sent to journalists to announce an upcoming event, such as a press conference, with the goal of securing media coverage.
An event where journalists are informed about the details of a particular issue or event, often including the opportunity for questions and answers.
A pre-packaged set of promotional materials for a person, company, or organization distributed to members of the media for promotional use, typically distributed as a digital document or web page.

The tracking of various media outlets and sources to find all relevant mentions about a company or certain topics; it can include monitoring newspapers, magazines, television, radio, and the internet.
The process of injecting your ideas or angles into breaking news, in real time, in order to generate media coverage for yourself or your business.
The element in a story that makes it newsworthy, timely, and of interest to the media and their audiences.
Information provided to a journalist that is not intended for publication. This agreement must be established prior to the information being given; otherwise, it is assumed to be on-the-record.
Part of a conversation with a journalist that can be reported on but not attributed directly to the source by name.
An article written by someone who is not the regular staff of a publication that expresses an opinion or perspective on a current issue.
A concise presentation of an idea for a story to a journalist or editor that outlines the main angles and benefits of the story.
The successful securing of a story, article, or mention of a person, company, or product in the media.
An event organized to communicate important information to multiple media outlets simultaneously, often allowing for a question-and-answer session.
Selected group of journalists from various media outlets who are designated to represent the wider press corps at an event due to space or security limitations.
A written statement to the media that announces something significant or newsworthy.
A secondary story or information accompanying a main story, providing additional details or a different perspective.
A short, catchy snippet or quote taken from a longer piece of audio or an interview that encapsulates the main point and is easy for the audience to remember.
Key messages designed to be emphasized by a spokesperson during an interview or media appearance.
A news agency that supplies syndicated news by wire to newspapers, radio, and television stations.

preface.para: In an era where museums are under unprecedented public scrutiny, the need for effective media relations has never been more critical.

A simple review of recent news media coverage about museums and institutional leadership reveals a field facing challenges never seen before in its history. Museums are under a microscope, and their leaders are often ill-equipped to handle the unexpected—and frequently negative—media attention. Compounding this issue is the fact that many museum executives have little experience and training in public relations (PR), and their institutions are often too small to employ a dedicated communications expert. This “perfect PR storm”has led to missed opportunities for positive promotion and some bungled PR responses that have resulted in tremendous reputational damage.

The goal of this book, Museum Flack, is to fill this critical gap. While there are numerous books in the museum field focused on marketing, membership, advocacy, fundraising, and audience attraction, a practical guide on museum PR and strategic communications is conspicuously absent. A search for such a resource turns up very little—only three books in the past forty years. Many museums lack the help or resources to understand the news media, social media, or crisis communications. This simple how-to guide is long overdue and needed now more than ever.

section.para: The primary purpose of this book is to provide museum professionals with the knowledge, skills, and strategies necessary to navigate the complex world of media relations effectively. Museums are custodians of culture, history, and knowledge, and it is essential that their stories reach a broad audience. Effective media relations can amplify a museum’s voice, attract visitors, secure funding, and enhance its reputation. This book offers a step-by-step approach to building and maintaining strong relationships with the media, crafting compelling stories, and managing crises. By the end of this guide, you will have a comprehensive understanding of how to leverage media relations to advance your museum’s mission and objectives.

You will gain practical skills in crafting compelling stories, pitching to the media, and managing crises. More importantly, you will develop a strategic mindset, recognizing that media relations is not just about getting coverage but about building long-term relationships and aligning media efforts with your museum’s mission and goals. This holistic approach will enable you to navigate the media landscape with confidence and achieve greater visibility and impact for your institution.
This book is designed for a diverse audience within the museum sector. It is particularly relevant for:

listitem.para: Museum Directors and Executives: Who need to understand the strategic importance of media relations in achieving institutional goals.
PR and Communications Professionals: Who are responsible for managing media interactions and crafting the museum’s public image.
Curators and Exhibition Managers: Who want to promote their exhibits and programs effectively.
Marketing and Development Officers: Who seek to enhance brand awareness and attract donors through positive media coverage.
Museum Educators and Community Outreach Coordinators: Who aim to engage the public and foster community relationships through media channels.
Students and New Professionals: Who are just entering the museum field and need foundational knowledge in dealing with the news media.

section.para: This book covers a wide range of topics essential for mastering media relations in the museum context. Each subject is explored in depth, providing both theoretical frameworks and practical applications to ensure a comprehensive understanding of media dynamics and effective communication strategies.

One of the foundational topics addressed is Understanding News Values. This section delves into what makes a story newsworthy and how museum professionals can align their stories with these values. By understanding the criteria journalists use to evaluate news, museum professionals can craft stories that capture media interest and resonate with the public.

Another critical area is Building Media Relationships. This section offers strategies for establishing and maintaining positive relationships with journalists and media outlets. It emphasizes the importance of trust and mutual respect, providing practical tips on how to become a reliable source for the media and foster long-term partnerships.

The book also covers Crafting Compelling Stories, offering techniques for creating engaging and newsworthy content. This section explores the elements of a good story, including narrative structure, emotional appeal, and visual components, to help museum professionals create content that stands out and captures media attention.

Media Pitching is another key topic, focusing on how to pitch stories effectively to different types of media. This section provides insights into tailoring pitches to specific outlets, understanding the needs and preferences of journalists, and using various tools and techniques to increase the chances of getting coverage.

In the realm of Crisis Management, the book offers best practices for handling negative coverage and managing crises. This section covers the importance of preparation, timely response, and transparent communication, providing a roadmap for navigating challenging situations and protecting the museum’s reputation.

The book also explores Leveraging Digital Media, highlighting the importance of utilizing social media and digital platforms to amplify the museum’s message. This section discusses strategies for engaging with online audiences, creating shareable content, and using digital tools to enhance visibility and reach.

Finally, the book addresses Measuring Success, offering tools and metrics for evaluating the effectiveness of media relations efforts. This section provides guidance on setting measurable goals, tracking media coverage, and analyzing the impact of media relations activities to ensure continuous improvement and strategic alignment with the museum’s objectives.

By covering these essential topics in depth, this book provides museum professionals with a comprehensive guide to mastering media relations, equipping them with the knowledge and skills needed to effectively communicate their stories, engage with the public, and achieve their institutional goals.

info.title: Ways in Which the Book Covers New Ground

section.para: This book presents a unique perspective by focusing specifically on the needs and challenges of museum professionals. While there are many general media relations guides available, few address the specific context of museums. This guide integrates real-world examples, case studies, and insights from experienced museum PR professionals to provide a tailored approach. Additionally, it explores the impact of digital transformation on media relations, offering strategies for leveraging new technologies and platforms to reach a broader audience.

Throughout the book, you will find real examples and case studies that illustrate the practical application of the concepts discussed. The content of this book is based on extensive research, interviews with museum professionals, and the author’s own experience in the field of media relations. The author has worked with various museums and cultural institutions, gaining firsthand knowledge of the challenges and opportunities in this sector. This background, combined with a thorough review of current literature and best practices in media relations, ensures that the information presented is both relevant and reliable.

As the reader will learn throughout this book, I was a journalist and editor for close to ten years before I moved “to the dark side” and started on my PR career path. It took a lot of on-the-job training, but being a journalist taught me a lot and made me a better communicator, starting with my writing style.

Strong journalism requires you to tell the news in the first sentence of the story. You want your story to be informative and capture the reader’s attention. You need to be concise and get to the point very quickly. Unfortunately, not all professions are taught this writing style. Lawyers or academics learn that they need to build their case, share a lot of history, and then the conclusion should be at the end of a paper.

Because of my background and training, I think it’s important to share the news at the beginning. I share this philosophy with the United States Military, which teaches an easy acronym called BLUF, or Bottom Line Up Front. If you want to more effectively communicate with leaders, co-workers, and stakeholders, just get to the point!

I didn’t learn this acronym until I started working closely with the active and retired members of the military. I started noticing “BLUF” at the top of emails, and it was followed by a simple sentence or two that provided the news or most important conclusion. According to a recent memo issued by Beale Air Force Base, north of Sacramento, California, not only does BLUF give the reader a quick summary of the issue, “it gives the option to either read the remainder of the email (with much more detail) or the reader may choose to skip the details being content with the summary (BLUF) provided. In addition to saving the reader time, it allows the message to be conveyed much more succinctly and, in many situations, precisely.”
Kelly Kendall, “Bottom Line Up Front,” Beale Air Force Base, February 10, 2012, https://www.beale.af.mil/News/Commentaries/Display/Article/280275/bottom-line-up-front/.

This method of communication is not exclusive to emails. This communication tool can be used in work conversations and meetings, as well. It’s even a good way to think about how you craft PR communications. It’s also a good tool from a leadership perspective. As the US Air Force memo states, “do you trust your people enough NOT to require every minute detail of a given situation?” Are you “down in the weeds”? If a summary of the issue at hand is enough, encourage your people to give you the BLUF. It’s also an effective presentation tool.

If you’re presenting to your colleagues, manager, or director, are you giving a straight answer? If someone asks, “What color is the sky?” you don’t need to describe how electromagnetic waves pass through the atmosphere. Simply stating that the sky is blue would suffice. Ask yourself the question, “Does my boss really need all of this information?” That’s why you are there. If you are working on a project, it is up to you to know the details. Give your boss the BLUF and if he or she needs additional info, they will ask.
As you saw at the beginning of this preface, I will include the BLUF at the beginning of every chapter to help the reader understand the main points.

info.title: Introduction
info.subtitle: Public Relations and Marketing Are NOT the Same Thing

listitem.para: Public relations (PR) and marketing are NOT the same disciplines or functions.
PR is a strategic communication process that builds mutually beneficial relationships between organizations and their publics.
Marketing is the process or technique of promoting, selling, and distributing a product or service.
PR and Marketing functions have different objectives and strategies, but they need to work together.

chapter.para: Throughout my career as a journalist, PR practitioner, and university professor, one of the most persistent misconceptions that has endured over the decades is the belief that marketing and PR are the same.

Whether you work at a museum, art gallery, or nonprofit organization, it is crucial for any leader to understand these differences. After reading this book, not only will you understand these distinctions, but you will also grasp the terminology, strategies, and tactics necessary to lead a PR plan for your organization or institution. More specifically, you will learn how to effectively tell your museum’s story to journalists with the goal of securing earned media coverage.

This book won’t transform you into a PR professional and should not replace the need to engage or hire a professional if you wish to develop a comprehensive PR strategy. Think of it as a textbook or how-to guide to help you speak the language of PR and ask the right questions. Before we go any further, let’s dispel the myth that marketing and PR are the same thing.museum PRdistinct role from marketingmedia relationsrole of PR professionalsmarketingdefinition and differences from pr

section.para:
According to the Public Relations Society of America (PRSA), the formal practice of what is now commonly referred to as “public relations” dates to the early twentieth century. Over the decades, it has been defined in various ways and has evolved along with the changing media environment. The earliest definitions emphasized press agentry and publicity, while more modern definitions incorporate the concepts of “engagement” and “relationship building.” In 1982, PRSA adopted the following definition: “Public relations helps an organization and its publics adapt mutually to each other.”
Public Relations Society of America, “About Public Relations,” Public Relations Society of America, https://www.prsa.org/about/all-about-pr. A more modern definition that stands today describes PR as a strategic communication process that builds mutually beneficial relationships between organizations and their publics.

PR involves anticipating, analyzing, and interpreting public opinion, attitudes, and issues that might impact the organization. It includes counseling management at all levels regarding policy decisions, courses of action, and communications, including crisis communications, while considering public ramifications and the organization’s social or citizenship responsibilities. PR efforts aim to protect the reputation of an organization through consistent research, conducting, and evaluating programs of action and communication to achieve informed public understanding necessary for the success of an organization’s aims. This may include marketing, financial, fundraising, employee, community, or government relations, and other programs. Planning and implementing efforts to influence or change public policy, setting objectives, planning, budgeting, recruiting, and training staff, developing facilities, and overseeing content creation to drive engagement and generate leads are core components of PR.

According to the American Marketing Association, marketing involves selling products or services and finding ways to deliver value for the company’s customers and audience. There are many different marketing strategies, including content marketing, email marketing, social media marketing, and influencer marketing. Through these various forms, marketing introduces the audience to a product or service that solves a problem they have. Over time, marketingmuseum marketing strategiesthis audience begins to form a relationship with the company and may eventually become customers.

info.title: What Is the Difference between PR and Marketing?

section.para:
The primary distinction between PR and marketing lies in their focus; marketing concentrates on selling products, while PR is dedicated to maintaining and enhancing an organization’s positive reputation. For a museum, this differentiation is critical to understand as it shapes both public perception and engagement strategies. According to the US Chamber of Commerce’s site “CO,” several key differences highlight the variance in daily activities, audience focus, goals, and success metrics between these two fields.
Jamie Johnson, “What’s the Difference between PR and Marketing?” U.S. Chamber of Commerce, October 29, 2024, https://www.uschamber.com/co/grow/marketing/differences-between-public-relations-and-marketing.

PR professionals within a museum context might be involved in developing compelling narratives about exhibitions, writing press releases for upcoming events, pitching stories to media outlets about groundbreaking discoveries or special exhibits, and managing relationships with journalists and media entities. Their goal is to build a positive image and foster relationships with stakeholders such as donors, community leaders, and the media, thereby enhancing the museum’s public image and societal value.

On the other hand, marketing professionals at a museum typically focus on promoting specific exhibitions, planning campaigns to increase visitor numbers, and conducting research to understand visitor demographics and preferences. Their target audiences are primarily the visitors, including families, tourists, students, and art enthusiasts, with the aim of maximizing ticket sales and participation in museum programs. Success metrics for PR in a museum involve measuring media buzz and the overall public image, whereas marketing relies on visitor numbers, revenue from ticket sales, and return on investment (ROI).

Despite having different objectives and outcomes, PR and marketing do overlap in certain areas. For example, both departments might use social media platforms to boost brand awareness and execute targeted campaigns for exhibitions. Their success is interdependent; if the museum’s brand awareness is insufficient, marketing efforts may struggle, and negative press can detrimentally affect visitor numbers.

An illustrative example of this synergy could be seen in a museum hosting a major traveling exhibition on ancient civilizations. The PR team might focus on securing positive media coverage and organizing press previews, while the marketing team implements promotional campaigns highlighting the unique aspects of the exhibition to attract visitors. By aligning these strategies, the museum can maximize its outreach and engagement, ensuring both departments contribute to a cohesive effort that strengthens the museum’s relationship with the public and enhances visitor experiences.

listitem.para: journalismstorytelling skillsOne of the key objectives of media relations is to get a journalist to cover your story.
In order to win over a journalist, you need to think like a reporter and understand their objectives.
Journalism and media relations are a lot more similar than they are different.
Key skills for both include: storytelling, critical thinking, strong writing, ethics, and time management.

chapter.para: The book’s title, Museum Flack, serves as a tongue-in-cheek nod to public relations (PR) professionals (“flacks”) and journalists (“hacks”). While these terms may seem informal or even derisive to some, they highlight the essential roles played by both fields in information dissemination. “Flack” describes PR experts tasked with managing public perception and sometimes dealing with criticism (“flak”), while “hack” refers to journalists who rapidly produce content, often facing pressure to prioritize speed over quality.

In the museum world, PR has become increasingly critical as institutions face heightened scrutiny. Many museum leaders, lacking PR expertise, struggle with unexpected negative media attention, missing opportunities to positively promote their work. The evolving use of “flack” reflects a broader responsibility beyond news mentions, aiming to counteract criticism, protect reputations, and restore image.
PR and journalism, despite their differences, maintain a crucial, mutually reliant relationship for information dissemination, each leveraging the other’s strengths to serve the public effectively.

section.para: I started my career as a reporter for one of the most important and influential trade magazines in the aerospace industry. I covered the business of airlines, airplanes, manufacturers, technology, and so on. In short, I covered almost anything that flew above the earth. I regularly interviewed business executives from around the world, as well as government leaders, regulators, safety experts, and more. I never went to journalism school, but I had a strong interest in the business world, I loved aviation … and I didn’t stop asking good questions.journalismethics and standardsjournalismattributes of skilled journalistsHow did I learn to become a reporter? First, I was an avid reader of the news. From a young age, I read the local newspaper from beginning to end, usually starting with the sports section. In high school, I became fascinated with the business world and started reading the business section of my local newspaper, as well as the Wall Street Journal.

I studied business at the American University and got my degrees in business management and marketing, which meant I understood basic finance, accounting, and economic concepts. At the same time, I worked at the university’s weekly newspaper and I loved writing. I wrote for the school paper and also wrote some freelance stories for some business newsletters and media. To my surprise, there weren’t many journalists who understood the business world and knew what questions to ask and how to report a story. My on-the-job training continued, and I worked as a journalist for almost a decade at several award-winning publications and media companies.

The way I describe my career path, I started as the original “Story Teller.” I worked to understand a story. I explored different sides and perspectives of a story. I used understandable words and concise language to explain a story for different audiences. When I moved to PR, I used the exact same skills. I spent a whole class in my university course explaining what skills and characteristics make for a strong journalist because the same skills are required to be an outstanding PR professional.

The attributes of a skilled journalist are numerous, reflecting a multifaceted role that encompasses being a reporter, storyteller, investigator, and guardian of the public interest. By honing these skills and upholding ethical standards, journalists perform an invaluable service, providing reliable information that forms the bedrock of a functioning democracy. Their work requires a commitment to continual learning and adapting to the evolving landscape of media and public discourse. Journalism is both a profession and a craft, combining rigorous ethics, the pursuit of truth, and the communication skills necessary to inform the public. A skilled journalist embodies several essential attributes and capabilities which distinguish them from their peers.

Curiosity is the driving force behind a journalist’s work. Skilled journalists possess an insatiable desire to understand the world around them, asking questions others might overlook and delving deeper into topics to reveal layers beneath the surface. This inquisitiveness fuels their search for the truth and propels them to explore various story angles. Adept research and investigative skills are also crucial. Skilled journalists know how to navigate complex information systems, distill data, and connect disparate pieces of information, conducting thorough investigations by sifting through documents, records, and databases to unearth facts that substantiate their reporting.

Ethical integrity is paramount in journalism. Respected journalists adhere to stringent codes of ethics, ensuring accuracy, fairness, and impartiality in their reporting. They avoid conflicts of interest, refrain from fabricating stories, and respect the privacy of their subjects when needed. In today’s digital world, technological proficiency is more important than ever. Skilled journalists are adept with various digital tools and platforms, from content management systems and social media to data visualization software. They understand search engine optimization (SEO) and know how to engage audiences across different media formats.

Strong writing skills are essential, as clarity in writing allows journalists to convey complex ideas in a way accessible to a broad readership. A skilled journalist has an excellent command of language and can synthesize information into coherent, compelling narratives without losing the nuance of the story. Great journalists are also talented interviewers, knowing how to ask the right questions, listen carefully, and create a rapport with sources. Whether interviewing a politician or a private citizen, they do so with respect and professionalism.

Critical thinking enables journalists to see beyond the obvious, allowing them to question the information they gather. It is crucial for discerning truth, challenging assumptions, and presenting a well-rounded perspective on each story. Adaptability and flexibility are also necessary as news never sleeps; skilled journalists must be able to shift between stories and beats, handle breaking news with composure, and adjust to new technologies and changing industry standards.journalismdigital transformation and evolution

Tenacity and determination characterize a journalist’s dedication to their craft, as stories often don’t come easy. A skilled journalist is willing to pursue leads for weeks, months, or even years, displaying the persistence needed to overcome challenges, adversity, and sometimes even danger. Communication skills are vital beyond writing. Whether pitching a story to an editor, explaining complex issues during broadcast segments, or engaging an audience during discussions, journalists must articulate their ideas clearly and confidently.

Networking abilities play a significant role. Building a broad network of contacts provides vital leads and insights that can make a difference in reporting. Skilled journalists cultivate relationships that support their work over time. Empathy and sensitivity are essential when approaching subjects. Understanding the impact their reporting can have on individuals and communities, journalists exercise care, especially when dealing with vulnerable subjects.

Attention to detail ensures that every fact is checked and every word is accurate, which is crucial for maintaining the trust of the audience and upholding the journalist’s reputation and that of their publication. Finally, effective time management allows journalists to juggle multiple tasks, prioritize stories, and deliver high-quality content on time, often under tight deadlines.

The basics of journalism have remained unchanged through the generations. The ability to write well, ask insightful questions, and meet deadlines were essential for reporters fifty years ago and are just as critical today. My career began as a reporter, where I learned these fundamental skills that have served me well. However, returning to a reporting job today would present significant challenges for me due to the many transformations journalism has undergone.

Journalism has experienced tremendous changes in recent decades, largely driven by technological innovations, shifts in consumer behavior, and the evolving nature of news dissemination and consumption. Among these changes, digital transformation has been particularly impactful. The rise of the internet and mobile technology has transformed journalism, with traditional print and broadcast mediums being supplemented or, in some instances, supplanted by digital platforms like websites, blogs, and streaming services.

Social media has become a major news source for the public, facilitating rapid information dissemination. Journalists today use these platforms to gather news, engage audiences, and expand their professional reach. Meanwhile, the advent of citizen journalism has empowered ordinary individuals to report news in real time, often from locations difficult for professional journalists to access, serving both as a complement and competitor to traditional journalism.

Journalism has embraced a multimedia approach, incorporating video, audio, and interactive elements to enrich storytelling and cater to varied audience preferences. Data journalism has emerged as a new facet, leveraging big data and computing power to translate complex datasets into understandable narratives. Additionally, algorithms now personalize newsfeeds, reflecting users’ past behaviors and preferences, altering consumption patterns but also raising concerns about echo chambers.

The financial landscape of journalism has also evolved due to declining print advertising revenues, leading to new models like digital subscriptions, paywalls, and crowd-funded journalism. The internet has ushered in a 24/7 news cycle, intensifying the pressure on journalists to deliver breaking news quickly and outpace competitors. Although long-form journalism faces challenges from the immediacy of digital content, some platforms have successfully carved niches for in-depth reporting.

Amid these changes, ethical and quality concerns have surfaced, with the speed of publication heightening the risk of misinformation and fake news, necessitating rigorous fact-checking. The role of journalists has expanded; today, they are curators, moderators, and sometimes even part of the story through live reporting and personalized content.

The evolution of journalism demands adaptability, critical thinking, and a steadfast commitment to integrity in the face of changing consumption habits and technological advancements. While the industry faces numerous challenges, these shifts have also opened the door to innovative storytelling methods and deeper audience engagement. Despite these changes, the core media relationsrole of PR professionalsjournalismsimilarity to PRprinciples of journalism—accuracy, fairness, and accountability—remain the bedrock upon which the profession continues to stand and evolve.

If you examine the lists of skills and attributes for PR and journalism side by side, you’ll notice significant similarities between the two professions. Both fields share skill sets, tactics, and principles, yet it is crucial to acknowledge that PR and journalism are distinct professions with different end goals. Understanding these commonalities is vital for professionals in both fields, as they frequently work closely together.

At the heart of both professions is storytelling. PR professionals and journalists craft narratives to engage, inform, and sometimes persuade their audiences. While their approaches may differ, a focus on compelling content is central to both roles. Strong writing and communication skills are also crucial for both professions. Conveying information clearly, concisely, and effectively is a common objective, requiring journalists and PR professionals to create content that is targeted, tailored, and adapted to various platforms and audiences.

Research is a fundamental component of both fields. Journalists conduct research to uncover facts, while PR professionals research to understand the media landscape, public opinion, and to develop informed communication strategies. Additionally, ethics form the backbone of both professions. Journalists adhere to truth and objectivity, while PR professionals are guided by principles of honesty and integrity in representing their clients or organizations. Both professions must maintain transparency and accountability in their interactions.

Understanding and focusing on the audience is another shared practice between journalists and PR professionals. Both must be attuned to audience needs, interests, and consumption habits to ensure their messages are received as intended. Building and maintaining media relations is essential for PR professionals, who rely on these relationships as part of their media strategy. Conversely, journalists often depend on PR contacts for access to sources, quotes, and information, creating a symbiotic relationship that fosters frequent interaction and collaboration.personalizationPR message targetingonline platformssocial media use in PRonline platformsreal-time communication

The digital age has revolutionized both journalism and PR, necessitating adaptation to the rapid development of social media, SEO, and multimedia content. Technological skills are essential for navigating the evolving digital media landscape. Crisis management is another area where PR and journalism intersect. While journalists might report on a crisis with an objective approach, PR professionals manage the messaging and communication to mitigate the crisis’s impact on their organization or client.

Although the objectives may differ—with journalists seeking information for a news story and PR professionals aiming to position their subject positively—both engage in interviewing. Skills to ask the right questions and gauge responses are important in both professions. Time management and deadlines are critical in journalism and PR. Effective time management is necessary to keep up with the fast-paced nature of news cycles and the timing of press releases or PR campaigns.

The intersection between PR and journalism reflects their shared foundation in communication, storytelling, and disseminating information to the public. Despite their differences, professionals in PR and journalism can learn from each other’s practices and perspectives, often leading to a dynamic and mutual relationship that benefits both fields.

info.title: Can PR Be Effective in Today’s Media Environment?

section.para: Considering how much the world of journalism and media has changed in recent years, alongside significant shifts in how people consume news, many wonder if PR can still be effective today. Absolutely, PR remains highly effective in the current media environment, perhaps even more so than before. The dynamic and complex media landscape offers numerous opportunities for PR professionals to craft and disseminate their messages effectively.

One key advantage is leveraging digital platforms, which have provided PR campaigns with unparalleled reach and precision. Social media, online communities, and digital publications enable PR messages to be tailored and targeted to specific audiences, yielding measurable results. Engaging content is also critical, as today’s media-savvy audience seeks content that adds value to their lives. PR professionals are adept at crafting stories museum leadersPR skill developmentthat resonate with the public, utilizing multimedia formats such as videos, podcasts, and infographics.

Influencer partnerships play a crucial role in amplifying a brand’s message. Influencers already hold the trust and attention of their followers, which can be leveraged for effective PR. Real-time communication is another vital aspect, as the 24/7 news cycle allows PR to be incredibly responsive. Brands can engage with breaking news and trending topics, providing immediate commentary or perspective to enhance visibility and relevance.

Personalized messaging has become more feasible thanks to data analytics, which enables PR strategies to become more personal. Understanding audience behaviors and preferences allows for communications that feel more relevant to each individual. Additionally, the interactive nature of modern media transforms communication into a two-way street. PR benefits from immediate feedback through likes, comments, and shares, which can inform and refine future strategies.

Crisis management has been revolutionized by the rapid dissemination of information. During a crisis, PR can manage the narrative effectively, executing crisis communication plans swiftly across various channels to mitigate any negative impact. Moreover, PR activities can enhance an organization’s online presence through SEO and online visibility strategies, improving search engine rankings and visibility.

Thought leadership is another significant aspect, where PR can establish company leaders as experts in their fields through opinion pieces, speaking engagements, and public discussions. This positions the brand as a trusted knowledge source. The global reach of PR campaigns has also expanded with the rise of online media, enabling them to reach international audiences without extensive physical networks.

In today’s intricate media environment, PR practitioners can leverage a multitude of tools and platforms to communicate their messages effectively. The key lies in understanding the nuances of modern media, staying ahead of technological advancements, and being willing to adapt to continuous change. By doing so, PR can remain a powerful force in shaping public opinion, managing reputations, and influencing perceptions.

info.title: How to Teach a Museum Leader PR Skills?

section.para: This guide is specifically aimed at individuals, such as museum leaders, who have little to no background in PR but are eager to understand enough to recognize and implement effective PR strategies. Teaching PR skills to someone who isn’t a natural communicator involves a combination of theoretical education and practical experience. Here’s how this book will help foster PR skills in a non-communicator within the museum context:

First, it is essential to introduce basic PR concepts. Begin with the fundamentals of PR, including its definition, purpose, and the differences between PR, advertising, and journalism. Highlight the importance of maintaining a positive public image and the impact of PR on a museum’s success, such as enhancing visitor engagement and community outreach.

Strengthening writing skills is a cornerstone of effective communication. Start with basic writing exercises that emphasize clarity, conciseness, and tone, particularly when creating museum newsletters, exhibition descriptions, and press releases. Gradually introduce various PR writing forms such as curator speeches, social media posts about exhibits, and op-eds advocating for museum-related issues.

Understanding the target audience is crucial in PR. Educate museum leaders on how to identify different audience segments—such as students, families, and art enthusiasts—tailoring messages to their values, interests, and behaviors to increase visitors’ interest and involvement. Public speaking can be daunting but is necessary for effective PR. Conduct mock interviews about museum exhibits and presentations for potential donors, providing constructive feedback on verbal and non-verbal communication techniques to enhance persuasion and engagement.

Highlight the importance of research by demonstrating how to conduct thorough research to understand trends in museum attendance, competitors’ strategies, and the media landscape. This knowledge will inform the creation of effective PR strategies for new exhibitions or public programs.

Emphasize strategic thinking by walking through the process of developing a museum PR strategy. Discuss setting objectives for visitor growth or community involvement, planning exhibitions, message development, and selecting appropriate channels and tactics for reaching different audience segments.

Developing media relations is crucial. Educate on the role of media in publicizing museum exhibits and events. Demonstrate how to build and maintain relationships with journalists, and how to pitch engaging and newsworthy museum stories effectively. Offer crisis communication training by explaining principles and stages. Role-play crisis scenarios, such as managing a sudden exhibit cancellation or controversy, to practice quick thinking and manage stressful communications effectively.

Use real-world examples by illustrating lessons with case studies from successful and unsuccessful museum PR campaigns. Discuss strategies used in these campaigns and lessons learned, helping museum leaders avoid similar pitfalls.

Promote ethical understanding by ensuring a clear grasp of PR ethics, such as transparency and truthfulness, stressing the importance of not misleading the public or media, particularly in cultural representation and conservation practices.

Encourage continuous learning by recommending that museum leaders follow PR blogs, listen to related podcasts, and join professional organizations to keep updated with the latest trends and practices in PR and museum management.

Finally, provide networking opportunities by introducing them to networking events and symposiums where they can practice interactions with other communication and museum professionals, fostering collaboration and innovation.

Transforming a museum leader from a non-communicator into someone proficient in PR skills is an incremental process. It requires patience, practice, and exposure to real-world situations. With consistent guidance and encouragement, even those who start with minimal communication skills can develop the competence necessary for effective PR work tailored to the unique needs of a museum environment.

In today’s fast-paced and interconnected world, the media landscape is more dynamic and influential than ever before. Whether you’re a seasoned PR professional, a museum leader, or a nonprofit advocate, understanding the intricacies of media relations is crucial for effectively communicating your message, building your brand, and managing your organization’s reputation.

Media relations is the strategic process of engaging with journalists, editors, and media outlets to secure positive coverage and convey your organization’s story to the public. It involves a range of activities, from crafting compelling press releases and pitching stories to arranging interviews and managing media inquiries. At its core, media relations is about building and maintaining mutually beneficial relationships with the media to ensure that your organization’s voice is heard and accurately represented.

This guide to media relations is designed to provide you with the knowledge, tools, and best practices needed to navigate the complex world of media engagement. Whether you’re looking to enhance your media outreach efforts, manage a crisis, or establish your organization as a thought leader, this guide will offer valuable insights and practical advice to help you achieve your goals.
