info.title: What Makes News and What Is Media Relations?

listitem.para: news mediarole in democracy and public discourseTraditional news media continue to play a crucial role in shaping public discourse, informing citizens, and holding power to account.
Agenda setting and framing are highly relevant to public relations (PR) because they directly influence how information is perceived and prioritized by the public and the media.
Journalists use several criteria—news values—to determine what constitutes news and what does not.
Media relations is the ongoing facilitation and coordination of communication and relationships between an individual, group, or organization, and the media.

chapter.para: In an era characterized by rapid technological advancements and an ever-evolving media landscape, the relevance and influence of the news media remain significant. Despite the proliferation of digital platforms and the rise of social media, traditional news media continue to play a crucial role in shaping public discourse, informing citizens, and holding power to account. Here are several reasons why we should care about the news media and why they remain influential.

section.para: One of the primary functions of the news media is to inform the public about current events, issues, and developments. This information is essential for individuals to make informed decisions in their personal and professional lives. For instance, during the Covid-19 pandemic, news media provided critical information about health guidelines, vaccine availability, and government policies, helping people navigate the crisis. Accurate and timely information from credible news sources enabled individuals to take necessary precautions, understand the evolving situation, and make decisions that affected their health and well-being.

A well-informed citizenry is the cornerstone of a functioning democracy. The news media serve as a watchdog, scrutinizing the actions of government officials, institutions, and corporations. By exposing corruption, malfeasance, and abuse of power, the media hold those in power accountable. Investigative journalism, such as the reporting on the Watergate scandal by The Washington Post, has historically played a pivotal role in uncovering political corruption and prompting significant political and legal consequences. Such reporting not only informs the public but also ensures that democratic processes are upheld by holding leaders accountable for their actions.

The news media have the power to shape public opinion by highlighting certain issues and framing them in specific ways. This agenda-setting function influences what people think about and how they perceive various topics. For example, media coverage of climate change has evolved over the years, with increased emphasis on scientific consensus and the urgency of addressing the issue. This shift has contributed to greater public awareness and support for environmental policies. By choosing which stories to cover and how to present them, the news media can influence public priorities and perceptions, thereby shaping societal attitudes and behaviors.

info.title: Providing a Platform for Diverse Voices

section.para: The news media provide a platform for diverse voices and perspectives, fostering public debate and dialogue. This inclusivity is essential for a healthy, pluralistic society where different viewpoints can be heard and considered. Opinion columns, guest editorials, and interviews with experts and community leaders allow for a wide range of perspectives on important issues, enriching public discourse. By amplifying voices from various news mediacombatting misinformationnews mediaadaptation to technologybackgrounds and communities, the news media contribute to a more inclusive and representative public conversation, ensuring that multiple viewpoints are considered in the decision-making process.

The news media play a role in preserving and promoting cultural heritage and educating the public about history, arts, and sciences. Through documentaries, feature stories, and special reports, the media contribute to cultural literacy and appreciation. Coverage of significant cultural events, such as the opening of a new museum exhibit or the anniversary of a historical milestone, helps to educate the public and preserve cultural memory. By highlighting cultural achievements and historical events, the news media foster a deeper understanding and appreciation of our shared heritage, contributing to the preservation of cultural knowledge for future generations.

The news media have demonstrated resilience and adaptability in the face of technological changes. While traditional print and broadcast media have faced challenges, many have successfully transitioned to digital platforms, expanding their reach and influence. Major news organizations like The New York Times and BBC have developed robust online presences, offering digital subscriptions, multimedia content, and interactive features to engage modern audiences. This adaptability ensures that the news media remain relevant and accessible in an increasingly digital world, allowing them to continue fulfilling their role as providers of reliable information.

In an age of misinformation and “fake news,” the role of credible news media is more critical than ever. Professional journalism adheres to ethical standards and fact-checking processes, providing reliable information that can counteract falsehoods and conspiracy theories. Fact-checking organizations public opinioninfluence via media framing and agenda settingframingrole in shaping public opinionand dedicated fact-checking sections within news outlets work to verify claims and debunk misinformation, helping to maintain an informed public. By providing accurate and verified information, the news media play a crucial role in combating the spread of misinformation, ensuring that the public has access to trustworthy sources of news.

The news media contribute to the economy by providing jobs and supporting related industries such as advertising, publishing, and broadcasting. Additionally, they play a social role by fostering community engagement and cohesion. Local newspapers and radio stations often serve as vital sources of information for their communities, covering local events, issues, and stories that might not receive attention from national media. By highlighting local news and events, the news media help to build a sense of community and connectedness, fostering social cohesion and engagement at the local level.

The news media remain influential and essential for several reasons. They inform the public, facilitate democracy, shape public opinion, provide a platform for diverse voices, preserve and promote culture, adapt to technological changes, combat misinformation, and contribute to the economy and social cohesion. In a rapidly changing world, the news media’s role in maintaining an informed, engaged, and democratic society is more important than ever. As consumers of news, it is crucial to support credible journalism and remain vigilant about the sources of our information, ensuring that the news media can continue to fulfill their vital functions. By recognizing the importance of the news media and actively engaging with reliable sources, we can contribute to a more informed and democratic society.

Agenda setting and framing are two powerful concepts in media studies that significantly influence public opinion. Both processes play crucial roles in determining not only what people think about but also how they think about it. It’s important to understand how these mechanisms work and their impact on public opinion.agenda settingmedia influence on public opinion

Agenda setting is the process by which the media determines which issues are considered important and worthy of public discussion. It involves the prioritization of topics that the media presents to the audience, thereby influencing what people think about.

By highlighting certain issues, the media can shape the public’s perception of what is important. Media outlets act as gatekeepers, deciding which stories to cover and which to ignore. The media agenda consists of the set of issues that are covered prominently by the media, while the public agenda is the set of issues that the public perceives as important. The policy agenda, on the other hand, includes the set of issues that policymakers consider important.

The process of agenda setting involves several steps. Media outlets select which stories to cover based on various factors, including newsworthiness, audience interest, and editorial policies. The amount of coverage and the prominence given to a story, such as front-page news or the lead story in a broadcast, also play a role. Frequent coverage of an issue can increase its perceived importance, and sustained coverage over time can solidify an issue’s place on the public agenda.

Mechanisms like priming and salience transfer are also at play. Media coverage can prime the public to evaluate political leaders and issues based on the topics that are most prominently covered. Salience transfer is the process by which the media’s emphasis on certain issues transfers to the public’s perception of those issues’ importance.

Consider the issue of climate change. If major news outlets consistently cover stories related to climate change—such as extreme weather events, scientific reports, and policy debates—this issue becomes more salient in the minds of the public. Over time, the public begins to see climate change as a critical issue that needs addressing. This increased public concern can then influence policymakers to prioritize climate-related policies.

In the early 2000s, media coverage of climate change was sporadic. However, as scientific consensus grew and more extreme weather events were linked to climate change, media coverage increased. Surveys showed a rise in the number of people who considered climate change a significant issue. This framingmedia presentation and impactshift in public opinion led to greater political pressure on governments to take action, resulting in international agreements like the Paris Agreement.

A museum-specific example of agenda setting can be seen in the Smithsonian National Museum of African American History and Culture’s (NMAAHC) role in shaping public discourse around racial history and social justice. By curating exhibits that highlight the African American experience, the museum sets the agenda for national conversations on race, identity, and civil rights. For instance, the NMAAHC’s exhibit on the history of slavery in America not only educates visitors but also influences public opinion and policy discussions by bringing attention to the enduring impacts of slavery and systemic racism. This agenda-setting role is further amplified through the museum’s public programs, educational initiatives, and partnerships with media outlets, which help to sustain and broaden the conversation on these critical issues.

Media framing refers to the way information is presented to the audience. It involves the selection and emphasis of certain aspects of a story to promote a particular interpretation or perspective. Framing can shape how people understand and interpret information, influencing their opinions and attitudes.

Framing affects how people interpret and understand the information presented. The choice of words, images, and context can influence the audience’s perception. For example, describing a protest as a “riot” versus a “demonstration” can lead to different public reactions.

The key components of framing include selection, emphasis, exclusion, and elaboration. Selection involves choosing specific facts, themes, and words to include in a story. Emphasis highlights certain elements of a story over others. Exclusion omits certain facts or perspectives, while elaboration provides detailed information on certain aspects while downplaying others.

There are various types of frames, including the conflict frame, which emphasizes conflict between individuals, groups, or institutions; the human interest frame, which focuses on personal stories and emotional angles; the economic consequences frame, which highlights the economic impact of an issue; the morality frame, which interprets issues in terms of moral or ethical agenda settingimportance in PR and newsconsiderations; and the responsibility frame, which attributes responsibility for an issue to individuals, groups, or institutions.

Mechanisms such as language and terminology, images and visuals, and context and background also play a role in framing. The choice of words can significantly influence perception, such as using “freedom fighters” versus “terrorists.” Photographs and videos can evoke specific emotions and reactions. Providing context can shape how an issue is understood, such as historical background or expert opinions.

Consider the issue of immigration. Media outlets can frame this issue in various ways, leading to different public perceptions and attitudes. For example, a conflict frame might have a headline like “Border Crisis: Clashes Between Migrants and Border Patrol,” focusing on confrontations, legal battles, and political disagreements. This may lead to perceptions of immigration as a contentious and divisive issue. A human interest frame might have a headline like “A Family’s Journey: Escaping Violence for a Better Life,” highlighting personal stories of migrants, their struggles, and aspirations. This may evoke empathy and support for more compassionate immigration policies.

An economic consequences frame might have a headline like “The Economic Impact of Immigration: Boon or Burden?” discussing the economic benefits and challenges of immigration, such as labor market effects and public services. This can shape opinions based on perceived economic outcomes. A morality frame might have a headline like “The Moral Imperative: Protecting Human Rights at the Border,” framing immigration in terms of human rights and ethical responsibilities. This may influence public opinion toward more humane and ethical treatment of migrants. A responsibility frame might have a headline like “Who is to Blame for the Immigration Crisis?” attributing responsibility to various actors, such as government policies, international relations, or migrants themselves. This can shape perceptions of accountability and influence policy preferences.

A museum-specific example of framing can be observed in the way the United States Holocaust Memorial Museum (USHMM) presents the narrative of the Holocaust. The museum carefully curates its exhibits to frame the Holocaust not just as a historical event but as a profound moral and ethical lesson for humanity. Through the use of personal stories, artifacts, photographs, and multimedia presentations, the USHMM frames the Holocaust in a way that agenda settingimportance in PR and newsemphasizes the human impact and the importance of remembering and learning from this atrocity to prevent future genocides.

For instance, the museum’s permanent exhibition is designed to guide visitors through a chronological journey, starting with the rise of the Nazi regime and ending with the aftermath of the Holocaust. This framing helps visitors understand the complex social, political, and economic factors that led to the Holocaust, while also highlighting the resilience and resistance of the victims. By framing the Holocaust in this manner, the museum not only educates visitors but also encourages them to reflect on the broader implications of prejudice, hatred, and indifference in contemporary society.

Focusing events are sudden, dramatic events that draw public attention to specific issues. These events can significantly influence the public agenda and policy discussions. Focusing events often act as catalysts for policy change or increased media coverage. These events are typically unexpected and have a significant impact on public opinion and media coverage. Examples include natural disasters, terrorist attacks, or major accidents that bring attention to related issues.

Agenda setting and framing are pivotal concepts in PR as they profoundly affect how information is perceived and prioritized by both the public and the media. These concepts enable PR professionals to effectively shape public discourse by ensuring that certain issues are prominently highlighted in media outlets, which ultimately influences public opinion. For instance, a PR professional who regularly pitches stories focusing on a company’s sustainability initiatives can propel environmental responsibility to the forefront of societal discussions, similar to how museums curate exhibitions that spotlight critical cultural or historical themes.

Moreover, the attention gained from media coverage can steer the course of policy and decision-making. When an issue, such as a public health concern, receives significant media attention, it is more likely to capture the interest of policymakers, potentially leading to increased funding and the implementation of new policies. In much the same way, museum exhibitions often inspire public and political discourse about important issues.

PR efforts are also crucial in building brand awareness, as securing media coverage for a company’s technological advancements can position it as an industry leader, akin to how museums can establish authority on specific topics through consistently well-received exhibitions. In times of crisis, effectively setting the media agenda can enable a company to control the narrative, focusing on resolution efforts rather than negative aspects—a tactic not unlike how museums may direct visitor focus toward positive societal contributions in challenging exhibitions.

Furthermore, the framing of stories plays a vital role in molding public perception. By presenting a new product launch as a revolutionary innovation, PR professionals can elicit enthusiasm and favorable reactions. This concept is mirrored in how museums frame exhibits to engage audiences and drive desired interpretations. During strategic business developments, such as corporate mergers, PR experts can frame the narrative to emphasize growth opportunities, resulting in more positive media outcomes.

Effective framing allows PR professionals to spotlight crucial elements of their message, enhancing their appeal. In press releases about charitable initiatives, highlighting the community impact and personal narratives can be comparable to museums showcasing impactful personal stories in their exhibits to evoke emotional connections. When controversy arises, strategic framing can diminish negative perceptions. For example, if a company faces criticism, presenting their decisions as necessary for long-term benefits can quell backlash, much like how museums might address contentious art pieces through thoughtful contextualization.

info.title: What Is an Influencer and Why Do We Care?

section.para: In the digital age, influencers have emerged as significant players in the media landscape, shaping public opinion, trends, and consumer behavior. Understanding who influencers are and how they relate to the news media is crucial for comprehending the modern dynamics of information dissemination and public engagement.influencersrelation to news media

Influencers are individuals who have the power to affect the purchasing decisions, opinions, and behaviors of others due to their authority, knowledge, position, or relationship with their audience. They typically have a substantial following on social media platforms and are seen as trusted sources of information and recommendations.

These are celebrities and public figures with millions of followers. They have a broad reach but may have less personal engagement with their audience due to the sheer size of their following. Example: Celebrities like Kim Kardashian or Cristiano Ronaldo, who have massive followings on platforms like Instagram and X (formerly Twitter).

Individuals with a large following, typically in the hundreds of thousands to millions. They often have a specific niche or area of expertise, such as fashion, technology, or fitness. Example: Popular YouTubers, bloggers, or Instagram personalities like Casey Neistat or Chiara Ferragni.

These influencers have a smaller, more engaged following, usually in the tens of thousands. They often have a strong influence within a specific community or niche, and their followers tend to trust their opinions highly. Example: Niche bloggers, local experts, or specialized content creators who focus on specific topics like vegan cooking or sustainable fashion.

Characteristics: Individuals with a very small but highly engaged following, often under 10,000 followers. They are seen as highly authentic and relatable, often engaging with their audience on a personal level. Example: Everyday social media users who are passionate about specific topics and have a dedicated, albeit small, group of followers.credibilityinfluencer credibility

info.title: How Do Influencers Relate to the News Media?

section.para: Influencers and traditional news media often play complementary roles in the information ecosystem. While news media focus on reporting and analysis, influencers provide personal insights, reviews, and lifestyle content. This complementary relationship allows for a richer and more diverse media landscape.

Influencers create content that can complement traditional news media. For instance, a news outlet might report on a new tech product launch, while a tech influencer provides a hands-on review and personal opinion on the product. This dual approach offers audiences both factual reporting and personal perspectives.

Influencers can amplify news stories by sharing them with their followers. This amplification can increase the reach and impact of news coverage, especially among younger audiences who may not consume traditional news media as frequently.

During major events like elections or social movements, influencers often share news articles, opinions, and calls to action, helping to spread awareness and mobilize their followers. For example, during the Black Lives Matter protests, many influencers used their platforms to share news updates, resources, and ways to support the movement. journalismethics and standardsinfluencerschallenges and ethicsanalysispublic opinion

Influencers act as opinion leaders, shaping how their followers perceive and interpret news stories. Their personal connection with their audience allows them to influence opinions and attitudes effectively.

Influencers discussing social justice issues, for instance, can shape their followers’ views and encourage activism and support for related causes. By framing issues in a relatable and accessible manner, influencers can make complex topics more understandable and engaging for their audience.

Influencers can bridge the gap between traditional news media and audiences who prefer more personalized and relatable content. They can translate complex news stories into more accessible and engaging formats.

An influencer might break down a complicated policy change into a simple, easy-to-understand video, making the information more accessible to a broader audience. This ability to demystify complex topics helps bridge the gap between traditional news reporting and everyday understanding.
News organizations increasingly collaborate with influencers to reach new audiences and enhance their content. Influencers can bring a fresh perspective and creative approach to news coverage.

A news outlet might partner with a travel influencer to create a series of stories about global destinations, combining journalistic reporting with personal travel experiences. Such collaborations can attract new viewers and provide a more diverse range of content.news valuesrelevance, timeliness, conflict, etc.news valuesdefinition and examplesnews valuescriteria for newsworthinessmedia coveragenews valueshuman interestdefinition and importance

While influencers can enhance news dissemination, there are challenges related to credibility and the potential spread of misinformation. Unlike traditional journalists, influencers may not always adhere to strict ethical standards.

An influencer sharing unverified information or biased opinions can contribute to the spread of misinformation, highlighting the need for critical media literacy among audiences. It is essential for followers to critically evaluate the information shared by influencers and cross-check with credible news sources.

Influencers play a significant role in the modern media landscape, complementing traditional news media by creating engaging content, amplifying news stories, shaping public opinion, and bridging gaps between news organizations and diverse audiences. Their ability to connect personally with their followers makes them powerful opinion leaders and valuable partners for news media.

However, the relationship between influencers and news media also presents challenges, particularly regarding credibility and the potential for misinformation. Understanding the dynamics between influencers and news media is essential for navigating the complexities of information dissemination and public engagement in the digital age. By recognizing the strengths and limitations of both influencers and traditional news media, audiences can make more informed decisions and contribute to a more informed and democratic society.

Journalists use several criteria to determine what constitutes news and what does not. These criteria help them assess the newsworthiness of events, stories, and information. Here are the key factors that journalists consider:
News is about what is happening now or has happened recently. The more recent the event, the more newsworthy it is.
Example: A breaking news story about a natural disaster that occurred today is more newsworthy than one that happened a month ago.
Events that occur close to the audience are more newsworthy than those that happen far away. Local news is often prioritized because it directly affects the audience.
Example: A local election in a city is more newsworthy to its residents than an election in a distant country.
The significance of an event or issue in terms of its effect on people. The greater the impact, the more newsworthy the story.
Example: A new law affecting healthcare for millions of people is more newsworthy than a minor policy change affecting a small group.
Events involving well-known people or institutions are more newsworthy. The actions of celebrities, politicians, and public figures often attract more attention.
Example: A statement by the president is more newsworthy than a statement by a local council member.

Stories involving conflict, tension, or controversy are often considered newsworthy. Conflict can arise from political debates, legal battles, or social issues.journalismdigital transformation and evolutioncrisis communicationPR strategiesExample: A high-profile court case or a political scandal is more newsworthy than routine government operations.
Stories that evoke emotions, such as happiness, sadness, or curiosity, are newsworthy. These stories often focus on individuals and their experiences.
Example: A heartwarming story about a community coming together to help a family in need is newsworthy due to its emotional appeal.
Unusual, rare, or unexpected events are newsworthy. The novelty factor makes these stories interesting and engaging.
Example: A story about a person surviving a rare medical condition or an unusual animal sighting is newsworthy due to its uniqueness.
Stories that are relevant to the audience’s interests, concerns, and daily lives are more newsworthy. Relevance can be determined by the audience’s demographics, location, and interests.
Example: A story about rising housing prices is relevant to a community concerned about affordable living.
Some issues become newsworthy because they are currently in the public discourse. These stories gain importance due to their connection to ongoing trends or events.
Example: During a pandemic, stories related to health, vaccines, and public safety are more newsworthy.news valuesevolution over time
News values have evolved significantly over history, influenced by changes in technology, society, and the media landscape. Here’s an overview of how news values have changed over time.

In the early days of journalism, newspapers had limited circulation and were often local or regional. News was heavily influenced by political and commercial interests, with newspapers frequently serving as mouthpieces for political parties or business entities. Due to slower communication methods, news was not as immediate, and stories could take days or weeks to reach the public. For example, early American newspapers like the Pennsylvania Gazette focused on political discourse, commercial advertisements, and local events.

The Industrial Revolution brought significant changes to journalism. Advances in printing technology and transportation allowed newspapers to reach a broader audience. The rise of “penny press” newspapers led to a focus on sensational stories to attract readers, with crime, scandal, and human interest stories becoming more prominent. The concept of journalistic objectivity began to take hold, emphasizing factual reporting and separating news from opinion. Newspapers like The New York Sun and The New York Herald popularized sensational stories and human interest pieces to boost circulation.

The advent of radio and television in the twentieth century introduced new ways to deliver news, emphasizing immediacy and visual storytelling. Journalism became more professionalized, with the establishment of journalism schools and codes of ethics. The rise of investigative journalism brought a focus on uncovering corruption, social issues, and holding power to account. The Watergate scandal, uncovered by journalists from The Washington Post, exemplified the power of investigative journalism in the 1970s.

info.title: The Digital Age (Late Twentieth Century–Early Twenty-First Century)

section.para: The internet revolutionized news delivery, making it instantaneous and accessible globally. Social media platforms became significant sources of news, allowing ordinary people to contribute to the news landscape through blogs and citizen journalism. The media landscape became more fragmented, with niche news outlets catering to specific interests and demographics. The emphasis shifted to breaking news quickly and stories that could go viral, sometimes at the expense of depth and accuracy. The Arab Spring (2010–12) demonstrated the power of social media in spreading news and mobilizing public opinion.

In the current media landscape, news organizations use multimedia elements like videos, infographics, and interactive features to engage audiences. Algorithms and data analytics allow news to be personalized to individual preferences and behaviors. The rise of misinformation and “fake news” has led to a greater emphasis on fact-checking and verifying sources. There is also a growing focus on diversity and inclusion, with efforts to represent a wider range of voices and perspectives in the news. News outlets like The New York Times and BBC use multimedia storytelling and interactive features to enhance their reporting, while platforms like Snopes and FactCheck. org focus on debunking misinformation.

The landscape of what constitutes news continues to evolve, driven by technological advancements, changing audience behaviors, and the dynamic nature of global events. While traditional news values such as timeliness, proximity, impact, prominence, conflict, human interest, novelty, relevance, and currency remain foundational, several emerging trends and factors are shaping what makes news today.

The digital transformation of the media industry has accelerated, with real-time reporting becoming the norm. News is now expected to be instantaneous, with live updates and breaking news alerts delivered directly to smartphones and other digital devices. Social media platforms like Twitter (now X), Facebook, and TikTok play a crucial role in disseminating news quickly, often outpacing traditional news outlets. This immediacy has heightened the importance of timeliness, making it a critical factor in determining newsworthiness.

The rise of user-generated content and citizen journalism has democratized news production. Ordinary individuals armed with smartphones can capture and share newsworthy events as they happen. Platforms like YouTube, Instagram, and Reddit have become significant sources of news, where viral videos and firsthand accounts can quickly gain traction. This shift has expanded the definition of what makes news, incorporating diverse perspectives and stories that might have been overlooked by traditional media.

In 2025, personalization and algorithm-driven news delivery are more prevalent than ever. News platforms and social media sites use sophisticated algorithms to curate content tailored to individual preferences and behaviors. This personalization ensures that users receive news that is most relevant to them, based on their interests, location, and past interactions. As a result, relevance has become a key determinant of newsworthiness, with stories that resonate personally with audiences gaining prominence.

The integration of multimedia and interactive elements has transformed how news is presented and consumed. News stories now often include videos, infographics, interactive maps, and virtual reality (VR) experiences to engage audiences more deeply. This multimedia approach not only enhances storytelling but also makes complex information more accessible and compelling. Novelty and human interest are amplified through these immersive formats, making stories more engaging and shareable.

In an era of rampant misinformation and “fake news,” the credibility and accuracy of news have become paramount. Fact-checking has become an integral part of the news production process, with dedicated teams and tools working to verify information before it is published. News outlets that prioritize accuracy and transparency are more likely to be trusted and followed. This emphasis on credibility influences what makes news, as stories that can be substantiated and verified are more likely to be covered.

Globalization has made the world more interconnected, and news that transcends national borders is increasingly significant. Issues such as climate change, pandemics, international conflicts, and economic crises have global implications and are of interest to a worldwide audience. Proximity, in this context, is redefined, as events in one part of the world can have immediate and profound effects elsewhere. Stories with global impact and relevance are thus more likely to be deemed newsworthy.

Social justice movements and advocacy for various causes continue to shape the news agenda. Stories related to human rights, equality, environmental sustainability, and social change resonate strongly with audiences, particularly younger generations. The prominence of these issues in public discourse ensures that they remain a focal point for news coverage. Conflict and human interest are often central to these stories, highlighting struggles, triumphs, and the quest for justice.

In 2025, what makes news is influenced by a blend of traditional news values and contemporary trends. The digital transformation, user-generated content, personalization, multimedia storytelling, fact-checking, globalization, and social justice movements all play crucial roles in shaping the news landscape.media coveragemuseum news trends
Understanding these factors is essential for journalists, PR professionals, and media consumers alike as they navigate the ever-evolving world of news.

The coverage of museums in the news has evolved significantly over the years, reflecting broader changes in media, technology, and societal interests. Here’s a detailed look at how news coverage of museums has changed through different eras.

info.title: Early Twentieth Century: Cultural Institutions and Elite Interests

section.para: Early news coverage of museums often emphasized their role as bastions of high culture and education. Museums were seen as institutions that preserved and showcased the finest examples of art, history, and science. Coverage was typically aimed at an elite audience, with articles appearing in cultural sections of newspapers and magazines that catered to educated and affluent readers. News stories often centered around major events such as new exhibitions, acquisitions of significant artworks, and visits by dignitaries. For example, coverage of the opening of the Museum of Modern Art (MoMA) in New York in 1929 focused on its innovative approach to modern art and its significance in the cultural landscape.

info.title: Mid-Twentieth Century: Expanding Access and Educational Role

section.para: As public education expanded, museums were increasingly seen as educational resources for the broader public. News coverage began to highlight their educational programs, school partnerships, and community outreach efforts. Coverage started to reach a wider audience, reflecting the growing accessibility of museums to people from diverse backgrounds. Significant cultural milestones, such as the opening of new wings or the acquisition of landmark collections, continued to be major news stories. The opening of the Smithsonian National Air and Space Museum in 1976 was widely covered, emphasizing its role in educating the public about the history of aviation and space exploration.

info.title: Late Twentieth Century: Blockbuster Exhibitions and Popular Appeal

section.para: The late twentieth century saw the rise of blockbuster exhibitions that attracted large crowds and significant media attention. These exhibitions often featured famous artists or culturally significant themes. Museums began to adopt more sophisticated marketing and promotional strategies, leading to increased media coverage and public interest. News stories started to highlight the role of museums in tourism and their economic impact on local communities. The 1978 “Treasures of Tutankhamun” exhibition, which toured several countries, received extensive media coverage and drew millions of visitors, showcasing the global appeal of blockbuster museum exhibitions.

info.title: Early Twenty-First Century: Digital Transformation and Interactive Experiences

section.para: The advent of the internet and social media transformed how museums engaged with the public. News coverage began to focus on digital initiatives, such as virtual tours, online collections, and interactive exhibits. Museums increasingly emphasized inclusivity and community engagement, with news stories highlighting efforts to make museums more accessible and representative of diverse cultures and histories. Coverage also began to address controversies and debates within the museum world, such as issues of repatriation, ethical collecting practices, and the representation of marginalized groups. The British Museum’s digital initiatives, including virtual tours and online exhibitions, received significant media attention, especially during the Covid-19 pandemic when physical visits were restricted.

info.title: Current Trends: Innovation, Social Justice, and Global Connectivity

section.para: Museums are leveraging cutting-edge technologies like augmented reality (AR), virtual reality (VR), and artificial intelligence (AI) to create immersive experiences. News coverage often highlights these innovations and their impact on visitor engagement. Museums are increasingly involved in social justice issues, using their platforms to address topics such as racial inequality, climate change, and human rights. Media coverage reflects these efforts, often focusing on how museums are evolving to meet contemporary media coveragepositive vs. negative coveragesocietal challenges. The global nature of the internet allows museums to reach international audiences, with news stories frequently covering international collaborations, traveling exhibitions, and the global exchange of cultural artifacts. The Smithsonian Institution’s “Race, Community, and Our Shared Future” initiative, which addresses racial inequality and promotes dialogue, has been widely covered in the media, reflecting the museum’s role in contemporary social issues.

The news coverage of museums has evolved from a focus on elite cultural interests to a broader, more inclusive approach that emphasizes education, community engagement, technological innovation, and social justice. As museums continue to adapt to changing societal needs and technological advancements, their coverage in the media will likely continue to reflect these dynamic shifts, highlighting their ongoing relevance and impact on the modern world.

info.title: Are Museums Getting More or Less Negative News Coverage?

section.para: The nature of news coverage for museums has become more complex and multifaceted in recent years, reflecting broader societal trends and changes within the museum sector itself. While museums continue to receive positive coverage for their educational and cultural contributions, there has been an increase in negative news coverage as well. Here are some key factors influencing this trend.

Museums are experiencing a mix of positive and negative news coverage, reflecting their evolving roles and the complex challenges they face. Negative coverage often stems from controversies related to ethical issues, representation, financial struggles, and public backlash. For instance, there has been growing scrutiny over the provenance of museum collections, particularly regarding artifacts acquired during colonial periods. Calls for the repatriation of cultural artifacts to their countries of origin have led to negative coverage for institutions perceived as resistant to these demands.

The British Museum has faced criticism and negative press over its reluctance to return the Elgin Marbles to Greece. Additionally, museums have been criticized for their lack of diversity in both their collections and their staffing, including underrepresentation of marginalized groups and failure to address systemic inequalities. The #MuseumsAreNotNeutral movement has highlighted issues of racial and social justice within museum practices, leading to critical media coverage.

Economic challenges, including reduced public funding and the financial impact of the Covid-19 pandemic, have led to negative news about museum closures, layoffs, and budget cuts. The closure of smaller museums and the financial struggles of larger institutions like the Metropolitan Museum of Art have been widely reported. Museums sometimes face backlash over controversial exhibits or partnerships, with public protests and social media campaigns amplifying negative perceptions. The Guggenheim Museum faced protests and negative coverage over its association with the Sackler family, linked to the opioid crisis.

Despite these challenges, museums continue to receive positive coverage for their educational contributions, technological innovations, community engagement, and cultural preservation efforts. Innovative and engaging exhibits that attract large audiences and enhance public understanding of art, history, and science are often praised. The immersive Van Gogh exhibitions have garnered widespread acclaim and positive media attention. The adoption of digital technologies, such as virtual tours and interactive exhibits, has been positively received, especially during the Covid-19 pandemic when physical visits were restricted. The Louvre’s virtual tours have been praised for making art accessible to a global audience.

Efforts to engage with local communities and create inclusive programs have been highlighted positively in the media. Museums that actively work to be more inclusive and representative receive commendations, such as the Smithsonian Institution’s community-focused initiatives and educational programs. Museums’ roles in preserving cultural heritage and conducting conservation work continue to be celebrated. The restoration of historic artifacts and artworks often receives positive media attention, showcasing the museums’ dedication to cultural preservation.

The increased scrutiny and critical coverage can be seen as part of a broader societal push for greater accountability, transparency, and inclusivity. As media relationsrole of PR professionalsmedia relationsdefinition and importancemuseums navigate these challenges, their ability to adapt and respond to public concerns will play a crucial role in shaping their future media coverage and public perception.

info.title: What Is Media Relations: Definition and Importance

section.para: Media relations is a strategic communication process that involves building and maintaining relationships between an organization and the media. It encompasses activities such as pitching stories, arranging interviews, issuing press releases, and managing media inquiries. The goal of media relations is to secure positive media coverage that enhances the organization’s reputation, informs the public, and supports its communication objectives.

Media relations play a crucial role in shaping and enhancing an organization’s reputation and credibility. Positive media coverage can significantly boost an organization’s public image, making it appear more trustworthy and reliable. When reputable media outlets cover an organization’s activities, products, or services, it lends third-party validation and credibility that is often more persuasive than paid advertising.

Example: A history museum that receives favorable reviews and coverage in cultural and educational publications is likely to be perceived as a valuable educational resource and gain trust from educators and history enthusiasts.

Effective media relations help build brand awareness by ensuring that an organization’s messages reach a broad audience. By securing coverage in various media outlets, organizations can increase their visibility and reach potential customers, partners, and stakeholders who may not be aware of their offerings.crisis communicationPR strategiescrisis communicationmedia relations roleExample: An art museum that secures media coverage for its exhibitions and collaborations with contemporary artists can enhance its profile and draw in diverse audiences who might be interested in its exhibits.

Media relations can influence public opinion by shaping how issues, events, and organizations are perceived. Through strategic messaging and media outreach, organizations can highlight their achievements, address misconceptions, and position themselves as thought leaders in their industry.

Example: A science museum that shares information about its STEM education initiatives and the impact on local communities can positively influence public perception of its contribution to societal development and education.

In times of crisis, effective media relations are essential for managing the narrative and mitigating negative coverage. By promptly addressing media inquiries, providing accurate information, and communicating transparently, organizations can maintain control over the situation and protect their reputation.

Example: A natural history museum facing controversy over the accuracy of an exhibit responds by engaging with the media to explain scientific evidence and clarify misunderstandings, thus managing public concern and maintaining trust.

Media relations support an organization’s broader business objectives by aligning media coverage with its strategic goals. Whether the aim is to launch a new product, enter a new market, attract investors, or advocate for policy changes, media relations can help achieve these objectives by generating positive publicity and raising awareness.
Example: A children’s museum promotes its newly opened interactive learning zones through media coverage, attracting more visitors and demonstrating its commitment to child education and engagement.

Media relations can position an organization’s leaders and experts as thought leaders in their field. By securing opportunities for interviews, op-eds, and speaking engagements, organizations can showcase their expertise and influence industry discussions.

Example: A science center or technology history museum regularly contributes expert commentary on the evolution of tech innovations and historical context to major science and technology news outlets, establishing itself as a forward-thinking institution.

Strong media relations involve building and maintaining positive relationships with journalists and media professionals. These relationships are built on mutual trust and respect, and they can lead to more favorable coverage and opportunities for collaboration.

Example: A museum’s PR professional consistently provides journalists with early access to new exhibit details, exclusive interviews with curators, and insider stories, building lasting relationships and increasing positive media exposure.

info.title: Importance of Building Relationships in Media Relations

section.para: Building strong relationships with the media is a cornerstone of effective media relations for several reasons. Journalists and media outlets have established audiences, and by building good relationships, organizations can leverage these platforms to reach more people than they could through their own channels alone. This access to broader audiences is invaluable for amplifying messages and increasing visibility.

When organizations maintain good relationships with the media, they are more likely to be the go-to source for stories, insights, and expert opinions related to their field. This opportunity for regular coverage can reinforce brand presence and credibility, ensuring that the organization remains top of mind for both journalists and the public. Having an established relationship broadcast journalismTV news story characteristicsask the expertLisa Starkcan mean quicker response times from both sides during urgent situations. For instance, in a crisis, being able to quickly get in touch with a journalist can help an organization shape the story effectively and promptly. This faster communication in urgent situations can be crucial for managing public perception and mitigating potential damage.

When journalists know and trust an organization, they are more likely to cover the organization’s news in a fair and detailed manner. This improved quality of coverage allows journalists to write more authentically about the organization, leading to higher quality and more engaging content. Such coverage can significantly enhance the organization’s reputation and credibility. Regular interactions with the media can provide valuable feedback on public perception and media impressions, guiding future strategies and messages. This feedback and insight are essential for refining communication approaches and ensuring that the organization’s messages resonate with the target audience.

Long-term relationships can evolve into partnerships, where media outlets may offer opportunities for features, special reports, or other collaborative content that can be mutually beneficial. These long-term partnerships can provide sustained media exposure and open doors to new opportunities for both the organization and the media outlet.

The effort invested in building these relationships often pays off with more accurate, fair, and favorable media coverage. It can also lead to a stronger overall reputation and greater influence in the public domain, making it a critical component of any effective media relations strategy.

Interview with Lisa Stark, an award-winning network news correspondent and veteran broadcast journalist. Stark was a national correspondent for ABC News for two decades. She then worked as a correspondent for Al Jazeera America, followed by Education Week and the PBS NewsHour. Stark was then the Assistant Vice President for Communications and Media at American University.

para.emphasis: Question: As a veteran TV news reporter, what are some characteristics of a strong news story?

section.para: journalismethics and standardshuman interesttv news featuresFor television news, the strongest stories are visual, may have conflict, and have a human interest element. They may have an urgency to them. They should be a story the audience can relate to, whether it’s national news or local news.

para.emphasis: Question: What is the average length of a TV news story? Why are they so short?

section.para: At the network level, some television outlets, such as the PBS NewsHour, will still run lengthy stories. But for the local stations or commercial networks, stories can range from one minute ten seconds to about two minutes. And a live report by a reporter may run about forty-five seconds. I remember when I covered the very last Space Shuttle mission—and the editors at World News Tonight gave me just fifty-six seconds to tell this historic story. (And yes, story lengths given to reporters can be that precise!) The network broadcasts are trying to get as many stories in as possible and likely feel that a viewer’s attention span is much shorter these days. And remember, a half-hour newscast has about seven to eight minutes of commercials, and lots of teases, so the news hole is quite small. It’s the same with local newscasts. The cable networks have a lot more time to work with, but these days they are all talk and very few taped stories.

para.emphasis: Question: Besides breaking news, is there room on TV news for feature stories that might be pitched by a museum or arts organization?

section.para: There is always room for softer features on TV news. Often the last story, called the “kicker,” has a softer feel to close out the newscast. Stories from any arts organization, though, can’t just be about a new exhibit or a new play. They must have a nexus to news. For example, the PBS NewsHour has a feature called “Art in Action.”They do stories at the intersection of art and democracy. A recent story focused on a theater group that takes classic plays to explore contemporary issues and problems. When I was at Al Jazeera America, I did a story with the National Portrait Gallery about an exhibit titled American Cool. As the museum put it, these were photos depicting “what does it mean when a generation claims a certain figure as cool? What qualities does this person embody at that historical moment?” So the story we were able to do was more than a story about a photo exhibit; it captured the meaning of American Cool through the decades.

para.emphasis: Question: What types of feature stories interest TV news?

section.para: Features that are highly visual or “feel-good” stories about human ingenuity or people helping others can interest TV news. Historical features can also be interesting, especially if they are setting the historical record straight. Local networks often have a lot more interest in feature stories with a local angle.

para.emphasis: Question: Did the growth of 24/7 cable news create more or less opportunities to tell news stories on TV?

section.para: When CNN first started in the 1980s, their reporters were reporting and writing stories. So, there was more opportunity to tell news. That model has gone by the wayside, and most of cable news these days is what we call “talking heads,” people being interviewed or reporters reporting live from an event, rather than pre-produced news stories. This is less expensive than shooting actual news stories and is likely not to change significantly.

para.emphasis: Question: How is the news for morning shows different than the traditional evening news?

section.para: If there is major breaking news, the morning news will cover it just as the evening news does. And not all morning shows are the same; some are more news-oriented than others. But for the most part, the morning news wants to start the audience off gently, and the subjects tend to reflect that. They also tend to be geared toward female audiences, with the (perhaps outdated) belief that women are the ones at home getting the children off to school. On morning news, you will see cooking and fashion information, a lot of celebrity news, and “news you can use.”
