info.title: What Is the Difference Between a Press Release and a Media Statement?

section.para: In the realm of PR, both press releases and media statements are essential tools for communicating with the media and the public. However, they serve different purposes and are used in distinct contexts. Understanding the differences between these two communication tools is crucial for effectively managing media relations and conveying the right message.

A media statement is a brief, focused communication issued by an organization in response to a specific event, inquiry, or situation. It is designed to provide a clear and concise message to the media and the public. Media statements are often used in situations that require a quick response, such as crises, controversies, or breaking news.
A media statement is typically shorter and more direct than a press release. It includes:

listitem.para: Headline: A brief title that summarizes the statement.
Introduction: A concise opening sentence that provides context for the statement.
Body: A few paragraphs that convey the key message, including any relevant details or quotes.
Contact Information: Contact details for media inquiries.

section.para: Example:
XYZ Museum Responds to Recent Vandalism Incident
FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE
Contact:
Jane Doe
Public Relations Manager

New York, NY—January 15, 2025—XYZ Museum today confirmed vandalism that occurred on the evening of January 14, 2025. Several exhibits were damaged, and the museum is currently assessing the extent of the damage.

“We are shocked and disheartened by this act of vandalism,” said John Smith, Director of XYZ Museum. “Our team is working diligently to restore the affected exhibits and ensure the safety and security of our collections. We are cooperating fully with law enforcement to investigate this incident.”

The museum will remain closed on January 15, 2025, to allow for a thorough assessment and cleanup. We apologize for any inconvenience this may cause and appreciate the community’s support during this difficult time.
For more information, please contact:
Jane Doe
Public Relations Manager

listitem.para: Press Release: Typically longer and more detailed, providing comprehensive information about an event, announcement, or development.
Media Statement: Shorter and more focused, providing a concise response to a specific event or inquiry.
Press Release: Used for major announcements, product launches, new partnerships, significant achievements, or upcoming events.
Media Statement: Used for quick responses to crises, controversies, breaking news, or specific media inquiries.media advisorypurpose and format
Press Release: Often planned and scheduled in advance to coincide with specific events or milestones.
Media Statement: Issued promptly in response to an immediate situation or inquiry.
Press Release: Includes detailed information, quotes, background context, and additional resources.
Media Statement: Focuses on the key message, with minimal additional details.

section.para: Both press releases and media statements are essential tools in the PR toolkit, each serving distinct purposes and contexts. Press releases provide comprehensive information about significant events and announcements, while media statements offer quick, focused responses to specific situations. Understanding the differences between these two communication tools allows PR professionals to effectively manage media relations and convey the right message at the right time. By leveraging the appropriate tool for each situation, organizations can enhance their communication efforts and build stronger relationships with the media and the public.

A media advisory, also known as a media alert, is a brief document used to inform journalists and media outlets about an upcoming event, press conference, or other newsworthy activity. Unlike a press release, which provides detailed information and context, a media advisory is concise and focuses on the essential details needed for media planning and attendance. The primary purpose of a media advisory is to encourage media coverage by providing journalists with the “who, what, when, where, and why” of the event.

info.title: Key Components of a Media Advisory

listitem.para: Headline: A clear and attention-grabbing title that summarizes the event or activity.
Subheadline (optional): A brief secondary headline that provides additional context.
Dateline: The date of the advisory.
Introduction: A brief paragraph that provides an overview of the event or activity.
Event Details: The essential details of the event, including:
Who: The key individuals or organizations involved.
What: A brief description of the event or activity.
When: The date and time of the event.
Where: The location of the event.
Why: The purpose or significance of the event.
Contact Information: Contact details for media inquiries and RSVP.

section.para: Example of a Media Advisory
MEDIA ADVISORY
XYZ Museum to Host Press Conference Announcing New Exhibit on Ancient Civilizations
FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE
Contact:
Jane Doe
Public Relations Manager

info.title: Beyond the Press Release: Media Relations Tactics and How to Decide Which to Use

section.para: While press releases are a staple in media relations, there are numerous other tactics that can be employed to effectively engage with the media and communicate your message. Choosing the right tactics depends on your goals, target audience, and the nature of your news. Here are some alternative media relations tactics and guidance on how to decide which to use, along with museum and non-museum examples.

Personalized pitches involve crafting tailored messages for individual journalists based on their interests, beats, and previous work. This approach demonstrates that you have done your homework and understand what the journalist is looking for.

listitem.para: When you have a specific story that aligns with a journalist’s interests.
When you want to build a long-term relationship with a journalist.
When you have exclusive or unique content to offer.

section.para: A museum launching a new exhibit on ancient civilizations might pitch the story to a journalist who specializes in history and culture. The pitch could highlight unique artifacts and offer an exclusive interview with the curator.

Media briefings are small, informal meetings with journalists to provide them with background information, updates, or insights on a particular topic. These briefings allow for more in-depth discussions and help build stronger relationships with key media contacts.press conferencesusage and planningmedia tourspurpose and examplesmedia relations tacticspress junketsmedia relations tacticspress conferencesmedia relations tacticsmedia toursmedia relations tacticsexpert commentary

listitem.para: When you have complex or detailed information to share.
When you want to provide journalists with context and background.
When you want to foster closer relationships with key media contacts.

section.para: A tech company developing a new AI technology might hold a media briefing to explain the technology’s capabilities, potential applications, and impact on the industry. The briefing could include a live demonstration and a Q&A session with the lead engineer.

Press conferences are formal events where an organization makes a significant announcement to the media. They provide an opportunity to reach multiple journalists at once and generate widespread coverage.

listitem.para: When you have major news or announcements.
When you want to address the media directly and answer questions.
When you want to create a sense of urgency and importance.

section.para: A pharmaceutical company announcing the approval of a new drug might hold a press conference to provide details about the drug’s benefits, clinical trial results, and availability. The event could feature presentations from the CEO and lead researchers.

Media tours involve traveling to different locations to meet with journalists and media outlets. These tours can be organized around a specific event, product launch, or campaign.media relations tacticsthought leadershipexpert commentarymedia relations tactic

listitem.para: When you want to provide journalists with firsthand experiences.
When you want to reach media in different geographic locations.
When you have a visually engaging story to tell.

section.para: A travel company promoting a new luxury resort might organize a media tour for travel journalists. The tour could include a stay at the resort, guided tours of the facilities, and interviews with the resort’s management.

Providing expert commentary involves offering knowledgeable spokespeople to journalists for interviews and quotes on relevant topics. This tactic positions the organization as a credible source of information.

listitem.para: When you want to establish thought leadership.
When you want to provide insights on industry trends or news events.
When you want to build relationships with journalists.

section.para: A financial services firm might offer its chief economist interviews on the impact of new economic policies. The expert could provide analysis and predictions, positioning the firm as a thought leader in the industry.

Thought leadership involves positioning an organization or individual as an authority in their field. This can be achieved through bylined articles, op-eds, white papers, and speaking engagements.storytellingplatform uses and strategysocial mediaengagement, monitoring, and platform usesmedia relations tacticssocial media engagementmedia relations tacticsmedia partnershipsmedia partnershipscollaborations with outlets

listitem.para: When you want to build credibility and authority.
When you want to share insights and expertise.
When you want to influence public opinion or industry discussions.

section.para: A healthcare organization might publish a whitepaper on the future of telemedicine authored by its chief medical officer. The whitepaper could be shared with media outlets, industry publications, and at conferences.

Media partnerships involve collaborating with media outlets to create mutually beneficial content. These partnerships can take various forms, such as co-hosting events, producing joint content, or sponsoring special sections.

listitem.para: When you want to reach a wider audience.
When you want to leverage the credibility of established media brands.
When you want to create in-depth or specialized content.

section.para: A museum might partner with a local newspaper to produce a special section on an upcoming exhibit. The section could include articles, interviews, and behind-the-scenes content, providing extensive coverage and promotion.

Social media platforms provide opportunities for real-time interaction and direct communication with media contacts. PR professionals can use social media to share news, engage with journalists, and amplify their message.media relations tacticssponsored contentmedia partnershipssponsored content

listitem.para: When you want to reach a digital-savvy audience.
When you want to engage in real-time conversations.
When you want to monitor and respond to media coverage.

section.para: A fashion brand launching a new collection might use Instagram to share sneak peeks, behind-the-scenes content, and live updates from the launch event. The brand could also engage with fashion journalists and influencers by tagging them and using relevant hashtags.

Sponsored content, also known as native advertising, involves paying for content placement within a media outlet. This content is designed to blend seamlessly with the outlet’s editorial content, providing valuable information while subtly promoting the organization.

listitem.para: When you want to reach a specific audience.
When you want to control the message and presentation.
When you want to provide in-depth or educational content.

section.para: A tech company might sponsor a series of articles on a popular tech news website, exploring the benefits and applications of its new software. The articles could include case studies, expert interviews, and practical tips.

info.title: How to Decide Which Tactics to Use

section.para: Deciding which tactics to use in media relations involves a structured approach to ensure that your efforts are effective and aligned with your op-eds and letters to the editordefinition, purpose, and strategycommunication objectives. First, define your goals by determining what you want to achieve with your media relations efforts. Are you looking to generate immediate coverage, build long-term relationships, establish thought leadership, or manage a crisis?

Next, understand your audience by identifying your target audience and understanding their media consumption habits. Consider factors such as demographics, interests, and preferred media channels. Assess the newsworthiness of your story by evaluating whether it is a major announcement or breaking news that may warrant a press conference, or if it is expert commentary and thought leadership content better suited for ongoing industry discussions.

Consider the media landscape by analyzing it and identifying the most relevant and influential media outlets for your story. Take into account the reach, credibility, and audience of each outlet. Leverage relationships by utilizing existing relationships with journalists and media contacts. Personalized pitches and media briefings can be effective for building and maintaining these relationships.

Budget and resources are also important factors to consider. Some tactics, such as media tours and sponsored content, may require more investment, while others, like social media engagement and expert commentary, can be more cost-effective. Finally, monitor and evaluate the effectiveness of your media relations tactics and adjust your strategy as needed. Track media coverage, audience engagement, and feedback to measure success and identify areas for improvement.

An op-ed, short for “opposite the editorial page,” is a written prose piece typically published by newspapers, magazines, or online platforms. It expresses the opinion of an author who is usually not affiliated with the publication’s editorial board. Op-eds are often written by subject matter experts, thought leaders, or public figures and are intended to provide a personal perspective on current events, social issues, or public policies.

Op-eds are a powerful tool for expressing opinions and influencing public discourse. While they offer significant benefits, such as establishing authority anecdoteshook in op-edsand advocating for change, they also come with challenges like limited space and potential public scrutiny. Understanding these pros and cons can help authors effectively leverage op-eds to communicate their messages and achieve their objectives.

Op-eds provide a valuable platform for shaping public discourse and influencing readers’opinions on important issues. By writing an op-ed, authors can establish themselves as authorities or thought leaders in their fields, thereby enhancing their credibility and visibility. When published in well-known outlets, op-eds can reach a broad and diverse audience, amplifying the impact of the message. They also offer an opportunity to advocate for specific changes, policies, or actions, potentially influencing decision-makers and stakeholders. Additionally, op-eds allow authors to engage in public debate, presenting their viewpoints and countering opposing arguments.

Op-eds typically come with strict word limits, which can constrain the depth and breadth of the argument presented. Authors may also face public scrutiny, criticism, or backlash, especially if the topic is controversial or polarizing. Additionally, the publication may edit the piece for clarity, length, or style, potentially altering the author’s original message. High-profile publications receive numerous submissions, making it challenging to get an op-ed accepted and published. Furthermore, the impact of an op-ed can be fleeting, as news cycles move quickly and readers’ attention shifts to new topics.

info.title: Keys to Writing a Successful Op-Ed

section.para: Writing a successful op-ed requires a blend of clear communication, persuasive argumentation, and strategic thinking. Op-eds are powerful tools for influencing public opinion, advocating for change, and establishing thought leadership. Here are the key elements to consider when crafting an effective op-ed.

The first step in writing a successful op-ed is selecting a topic that is timely, relevant, and compelling. The topic should resonate with the audience and address current events, social issues, or public policies. It should also be something the author is passionate about and knowledgeable in, as this will lend credibility and authenticity to the piece. A clear and concise thesis statement is the backbone of any op-ed. The thesis should present the main argument or perspective in a single, powerful sentence. It should be specific, debatable, and reflect the author’s unique viewpoint. A strong thesis helps to focus the op-ed and provides a roadmap for the reader.The opening of an op-ed is crucial for capturing the reader’s attention. Start with a hook that draws the reader in, such as a provocative question, a surprising fact, a personal anecdote, or a compelling quote. The introduction should set the stage for the argument and make the reader want to continue reading. A successful op-ed is built on a foundation of solid evidence and logical reasoning. Use data, statistics, expert opinions, and real-world examples to support the main argument. This not only strengthens the credibility of the piece but also helps to persuade the reader. Be sure to cite sources accurately and avoid making unsupported claims.

Op-eds are typically short, with strict word limits, so clarity and conciseness are essential. Use simple, direct language, and avoid jargon or overly complex sentences. Each paragraph should focus on a single idea, and transitions should be smooth to maintain the flow of the argument. Aim to make every word count. Anticipating and addressing counterarguments demonstrates thorough understanding and strengthens the op-ed. Acknowledge opposing viewpoints and provide reasoned responses to them. This shows that the author has considered multiple perspectives and is prepared to defend their position.

A strong conclusion reinforces the main argument and leaves a lasting impression on the reader. Summarize the key points and restate the thesis in a powerful way. End with a call to action, urging readers to take specific steps, whether it’s supporting a policy, changing a behavior, or simply thinking differently about an issue. Each publication has its own guidelines for op-ed submissions, including word count, format, and contact information. Adhering to these guidelines increases the chances of acceptance. Research the target publication’s audience and editorial style to tailor the op-ed accordingly.

Keep in mind that an op-ed is not meant to be a sales pitch with a lot of marketing language about your organization. An op-ed that sounds like a marketing piece that is focused on promoting your organization (or disparaging a competitor) will likely be rejected by most news organizations. Editing and revising are critical steps in the writing process. Review the op-ed for clarity, coherence, and conciseness. Check for grammatical errors, typos, and inconsistencies. It can be helpful to have a colleague or mentor review the piece and provide feedback. Multiple revisions may be necessary to refine the argument and polish the writing.

According to an August 2024 report in Axios Communicators,
https://www.axios.com/newsletters/axios-communicators-f0ce76e0-5016-11ef-a435-e3ff58a9b123.html?utm_source=newsletter&utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=newsletter_axioscommunicators&stream=business. major news publications are closing their opinion sections, compelling business leaders, elected officials, and subject matter experts to directly communicate their messages. This shift is significant because, unless you are a high-profile figure like George Clooney or Jamie Dimon, your op-eds are unlikely to be accepted and even less likely to spark conversation. The trend of agenda setting is increasingly moving to social media, with many executives turning to LinkedIn to share their thoughts and opinions. LinkedIn has reported a 23 percent increase in posts from chief executives over the past year, resulting in a 39 percent increase in followers for CEOs. On average, CEO posts receive eight times more impressions and four times more engagements than other posts, according to LinkedIn data shared with Axios.

For instance, Ford CEO Jim Farley’s recent LinkedIn op-ed received coverage in Barron’s and Electrek, while Spotify CEO Daniel Ek’s posts garnered 5.3 million impressions and over 130,000 new followers in his first nine months on the platform, continuing to attract media attention. Other executives, such as Bastian, former Starbucks CEO Howard Schultz, and Pfizer’s Albert Bourla, are also using direct communication methods.

Despite this trend, publishing an op-ed in a major national publication still holds significant value and guarantees a wide audience. Memo readership data shared with Axios indicates that New York Times opinion articles had 37 percent more readers than its general news coverage in the last thirty days, while Wall Street Journal op-eds attracted 571 percent more readers than its general news.

However, the chances of securing such placements are diminishing due to the shrinking media landscape, according to Alex Sommer, senior vice president and associate counsel at Tusk Strategies. Sommer notes that the market for business leaders to share their views is now bifurcated, with only a few remaining media avenues like the Wall Street Journal, the New York Times, and the Washington Post for broad national reach, and local op-eds still being impactful from a public affairs standpoint. Recently, CNN closed its opinion section amid newsroom restructuring, and Gannett, the publisher of letters to the editorpurpose and usagehundreds of local newspapers and USA Today, announced it would reduce opinion columns. Many newer digital outlets like Punchbowl News, Puck, and Axios never launched opinion pages.

Critics argue that opinion pages can harm journalistic integrity and blur the lines between editorial and paid content. Despite these challenges, there are still over 1,100 US-based news outlets that accept outside contributor content, according to Muck Rack’s database. TIME has increased its investment in thought leadership with the launch of TIME 100 Voices, US News and World Report has expanded its opinion desk, and Forbes has long monetized its thought leadership offerings through its Forbes Councils.

info.title: What Is a Letter to the Editor?

section.para: A letter to the editor is a short, written communication sent to a newspaper, magazine, or other publication to express opinions, provide feedback, or comment on issues of public interest. These letters are typically written by readers and can address recent articles, current events, or broader societal issues. They are usually concise and aim to contribute to public dialogue or influence public opinion.

Writing a letter to the editor offers several advantages. It provides a public platform to voice opinions and share perspectives on important issues, encouraging community engagement and participation in public discourse, which fosters a sense of involvement and activism. Such letters can influence public opinion and raise awareness about specific issues, potentially swaying readers’ views. They also allow for a timely response to recent articles or events, keeping the conversation current and relevant. Additionally, letters to the editor are generally accessible to a wide range of people, as most publications welcome letters from their readership.

However, there are also some drawbacks to writing a letter to the editor. Letters are often subject to strict word limits, which can restrict the depth and detail of the argument. Editors have the discretion to select which letters are published, and they may edit for clarity, length, or style, potentially altering the original message. Authors may face public exposure and potential backlash, especially if the topic is controversial. Letters to the editor typically have a short lifespan, as they are often published in a single issue and then replaced ask the expertKate Meissnerby new content. Additionally, there is high competition for publication space, meaning that not all letters will be published, and those that are may not reach a wide audience.

Letters to the editor are a valuable tool for individuals to engage in public discourse, express opinions, and influence public opinion. While they offer benefits such as providing a public platform and encouraging community engagement, they also come with challenges like limited space and editorial discretion. Understanding these pros and cons can help individuals effectively use letters to the editor to communicate their views and contribute to public dialogue.

Interview with Kate Meissner, partner at Velocity Partners. Kate has deep media experience, including leadership roles at Politico and Axios. Previously, she was the youngest EVP at Edelman. Kate started her career as a consultant at Oliver Wyman, focused on intersection points between regulation and
Wall Street.

para.emphasis: Q: How do media get their news story ideas?

section.para: Many seasoned reporters with a developed beat get their story ideas purely from networking—from having conversations with their sources and developing hypotheses on what may or may not be happening in a space, then verifying those hypotheses in the course of their reporting. An increasing number of reporters also say they’re getting their story ideas from social media. My experience is that this is more true among junior reporters and in the trade media space.

Q: Are press releases still an important public relations tool? While I rarely advise a client to put anything on the wire anymore, I do think that press releases are a strong forcing function to create the appropriate news arc and contextualize the piece of news you’re looking to convey. Reporters will often write from the release, so it’s your first opportunity to shape the narrative, especially when a reporter has an exclusive. Often, I write a release simply to send to whoever is taking an exclusive story I’m placing.

para.emphasis: Q: If so, what are the key components of a press release?

listitem.para: Headline: Tells readers what the release is about and grabs their attention
Summary: Summarizes the key points in the release and should complement the headline
Time and location: Says when and from where the news is being released

Body copy: shapes the overall narrative of the news being released, placing it in context of additional information relevant to the story, including quotes from executives and others relevant to the news
Boilerplate: quick “about us” overview of the company

para.emphasis: Q: What are the most important parts of a release?

section.para: I have personally always felt that the most important piece is the summary or subhead—headlines are usually straightforward to write, but the summary piece is what really shapes the reporter’s perspective on what the news is.

I also can’t underscore this enough: every word, of every release, should say something. It’s a tight format where economy of language is important, and a (rare) opportunity to truly shape your own narrative before going to media.

para.emphasis: Q: What’s the difference between a media advisory, a press release, and a press statement? When should I use these tools?

section.para: A media advisory is sent when you have an event that you want media to show up—it informs them where, when, and by whom news will be broken. If a reporter wants to break the news, he or she will show up to the event.
A press release breaks the news with its writing—giving the reporter enough to report a quick story with one single piece of content.

A press statement is a statement provided to the response, usually in response to an inquiry. Oftentimes, I have done this as a “holding statement,” that is, prepared in advance on a topic that may have inquiries and provided if inquiries arise. This helps avoid the dreaded “could not be immediately reached for comment” line.

para.emphasis: Q: If I don’t have hard news, what are some other tools to get my story in front of a journalist?

section.para: Contextualize it into a story that they’re telling. For example, the WSJ probably won’t write about your client’s new headquarters. But they may write a business trend story about multiple companies moving to a specific “hot” location or adopting a specific office format. This type of pitch often requires finding additional sources to provide back to a reporter and a personal relationship with the reporter you’re pitching, but it can be a powerful way to shape top-tier media.
Q: What are some of the most effective tactics that you’ve seen? Two conflicting things on this.

First, it’s become commonplace to pooh-pooh personal relationships with reporters, but I continue to think they are the best way to get coverage. You don’t need to be wining and dining people, but my experience has always been that the best media relations comes from becoming the source—giving a reporter valuable information and context on an industry or topic so that they’re calling you in addition to you calling them. As you develop reporter relationships, it’s important to keep an eye out for what they’re looking for and find ways to help them however possible. They’ll be more receptive to helping you (or your client) when you need it.

Second, you really do have to do your research. Understand who’s covering what, who’s interested in what, what career aspirations specific reporters appear to have with their beats. If you can understand what drives them and moves them, you’re much more likely to have success in your pitches. Often I do this both by reading coverage and by doing my own “reporting”—calling other comms people I know who have been in this space and can tell me who cares about what, who’s fair, and who’s most willing to take specific types of pitches. When I get a new client, calling around to get smart on their space is the first thing I do. Just like a reporter would source up on a new beat, you have to be able to quickly spin up on a space and its angles.

Tactically but importantly—I think a lot of reporters have largely started ignoring email as a matter of course. Junior PR people often complain to me that it’s so hard to get in touch with reporters—and to this, I say that my secret isn’t necessarily relationships but often tactics. In addition to doing my research, I do a lot of pitching off of email—I direct message (DM) on X (fomerly Twitter), I use Signal and tools like Protonmail, I comment when reporters post their stories on LinkedIn, and if I have a personal relationship, I often open a pitch with a text, then follow through with more details.

para.emphasis: Q: Now that news is delivered digitally more than ever, do we need to change our PR tactics?

section.para: 100 percent. I’m a big fan of clients going direct-to-audience in addition to more traditional PR tactics. It’s a smart move for your CEO to consistently be posting on LinkedIn and writing on Medium, at minimum. That said, I will always maintain that there’s a unique space for real placements. Getting a client an interview or feature in a reputable publication can supercharge their reputation and B2B and B2C marketing in a way that owned media simply can’t. Earned media is evidence of credibility.

Q: Does the audience or message change what tactics we use? Yes! For policymakers and regulators, often the most effective tactic is either an inside-the-Beltway media play (Politico, Punchbowl, Axios) or, in many cases, convenings. For investors, it’s a similar story but with a different media set (CNBC, WSJ, Bloomberg) and investor day convenings. For a consumer message, the move now is often an influencer campaign or something stunty—as many like to say, TikTok is the new editorial calendar.

From a media perspective, it’s important to remember that there are many different types of reporters, and appealing to them feels different. Often, I find myself simultaneously working with top-tier reporters (where you really have to nail your pitch and give additional sourcing and context that matters to them), trade media (where you can be a bit looser), and more features-oriented publications (where there are even fewer watchouts).

para.emphasis: Q: I work at a museum and we only issue press releases, and the only subject of the release is announcing new exhibits. What other topics and tactics should we consider?

section.para: It depends on your goals. If you’re trying to raise money, consider pitching a longer-form feature that can serve as a tool in your fundraising campaign. If you’re looking to bring more foot traffic into the museum, consider a social campaign or a built-for-TikTok stunt that results in earned media. Consider taking actions that can result in communications campaigns to drive your reputation—for example, making the museum free for a day and pitching a local news story about it, or providing a docent-training program to students from underserved communities.

para.emphasis: Q: Is social media still an effective tactic/distribution channel to reach news media?

section.para: I would argue it’s necessary but not sufficient. Yes, you should have active social channels and make full use of them—but I wouldn’t leave it there. As the number of reporters continues to decline, the personalized tactics I mentioned above are even more critical than they used to be. Don’t assume someone is going to write about this or pick it up just because you put it on your social channels.

listitem.para: The rise of digital media has led to a decline in print readership, with many traditional publications transitioning to digital formats. Online platforms, including news websites, social media, and apps, now dominate as primary news sources.

Platforms like Facebook, X (formerly Twitter), YouTube, and Instagram have become major news sources, enabling real-time updates and interactive engagement, often outpacing traditional media in speed and reach.
Algorithms personalizing news feeds based on user behavior are creating tailored news experiences, though they risk creating echo chambers by limiting exposure to diverse viewpoints.
The ease of online content sharing has increased misinformation risks, making media literacy and fact-checking critical in navigating this new media landscape.

For public relations (PR) professionals in museums and beyond, understanding these changes is crucial for adapting communication strategies effectively and engaging with audiences across multiple platforms.

chapter.para: The landscape of news consumption in America has transformed dramatically over the past few decades, influenced by technological advancements, changes in media ownership, and evolving consumer preferences. This shift has significant implications for PR professionals who must adapt their strategies to effectively reach and engage their target audiences. Here, we delve deeper into the key trends and changes in how Americans consume news.

Historically, newspapers and magazines were the primary sources of news for Americans. However, the advent of the internet and digital technologies has led to a significant decline in print media readership. Many traditional print media landscapechanges in news consumptionfilm and video contentimportance in newsdigital medianews consumption trendsalgorithmspersonalizing news feedspublications have either transitioned to digital formats or ceased operations altogether. This decline is attributed to several factors. Digital news is more accessible and convenient, allowing readers to access information anytime and anywhere. Additionally, digital news is often free or cheaper than print subscriptions, making it more attractive to consumers. Growing awareness of environmental issues has also led some consumers to prefer digital over print to reduce paper waste.

The internet has revolutionized the way news is disseminated and consumed. A significant portion of Americans now get their news from online sources, including news websites, social media platforms, and news apps. This shift has been driven by the speed and timeliness of online news, which can be updated in real time, providing immediate access to breaking news and developments. Digital platforms also allow for interactive features such as comments, shares, and likes, fostering greater engagement with the content. Moreover, the internet offers a wide range of news sources, allowing consumers to access diverse viewpoints and niche topics.

Social media platforms have become major sources of news for many Americans. Platforms like Facebook, X (formerly Twitter), Instagram, YouTube, and TikTok enable users to share and consume news quickly and easily. Social media allows ordinary users to share news and information, sometimes even breaking news before traditional media outlets. News stories can go viral on social media, reaching a vast audience in a short amount of time. Influencers and citizen journalists on social media can shape public opinion and drive news coverage.

The proliferation of smartphones and tablets has made it easier for people to access news on the go. Mobile-friendly news apps and websites are increasingly popular, and features like push notifications ensure that users receive timely updates. Mobile devices allow users to access news anytime and anywhere, fitting seamlessly into their daily routines. Many news apps offer personalized news feeds based on user preferences and behavior. Mobile platforms support a variety of content types, including articles, videos, and infographics.

There is a growing preference for video content among news consumers. Platforms like YouTube, Facebook, and news websites offer video news segments, and live streaming of events and news broadcasts has become more common. Video content is often more engaging and easier to consume storytellingplatform uses and strategysocial mediaengagement, monitoring, and platform usesmedia relations tacticsdigital PRdigital mediaengagement tacticsdigital mediadigital PRaudience engagementsocial media interactionalgorithmspersonalizing news feedsthan text-based articles. Live streaming allows for real-time coverage of events, providing an immersive experience for viewers. Video platforms often include interactive features such as live chats and polls, enhancing viewer engagement.

Many digital news platforms use algorithms to personalize news feeds based on user preferences and behavior. This can lead to a more tailored news experience. News platforms use algorithms to curate content that aligns with users’ interests and past behavior. Services like Google News and Apple News aggregate news from various sources, allowing users to customize their news consumption. While personalization can enhance the user experience, it can also create echo chambers where users are exposed only to information that reinforces their existing beliefs.

The rise of digital and social media has also led to concerns about misinformation and the spread of fake news. This has made media literacy and fact-checking more important than ever. The ease of sharing information online has led to the rapid spread of false or misleading news. Trust in traditional media has fluctuated, with some Americans expressing skepticism toward mainstream news outlets. This has led to a diversification of news sources. Fact-checking organizations and tools have become essential in combating misinformation and ensuring the accuracy of news.

News consumption habits vary significantly across different demographic groups. Understanding these differences is crucial for tailoring PR strategies. Younger generations are more likely to consume news online and through social media, while older generations may still rely more on traditional media like TV and print. Different demographic groups may prefer different platforms. For example, younger users might favor Instagram and TikTok, while older users might prefer Facebook and Twitter. Preferences for content types (e.g., articles, videos, podcasts) can also vary by demographic group.

According to the Pew Research Center, as of recent years, a majority of Americans get their news from digital devices, with social media being a significant source. Television remains a major source of news, especially for older demographics, but its dominance is waning compared to digital sources.media relations tacticssocial media engagementdigital mediacontent diversityaudience engagementsocial media interaction

section.para: The changing landscape of news consumption has several implications for PR professionals:

listitem.para: Multi-Platform Strategies: PR professionals need to adopt multi-platform strategies to reach diverse audiences effectively. This includes leveraging both traditional and digital media.

Engagement and Interaction: Engaging with audiences on social media and other digital platforms is crucial for building relationships and trust. This involves responding to comments, participating in discussions, and using interactive features.
Content Variety: Creating a variety of content types, including articles, videos, infographics, and live streams, can help capture the attention of different audience segments.
Monitoring and Analytics: Using digital tools to track coverage, audience engagement, and sentiment analysis can provide valuable insights for refining PR strategies.
Credibility Management: Being mindful of the varying credibility levels of digital outlets and choosing where to place stories accordingly is essential for maintaining a positive reputation.

section.para: In conclusion, the way Americans consume news has evolved significantly, with a clear shift toward digital and mobile platforms, increased use of social media, and a growing preference for personalized and multimedia content. PR professionals must adapt to these changes by developing multi-platform strategies, engaging with audiences in real time, and creating diverse and engaging content to effectively reach and influence their target audiences.

info.title: How Do We Adapt PR Strategies?

section.para: Adapting to the evolving landscape of news consumption requires PR professionals in museums to develop innovative strategies that leverage digital platforms, engage diverse audiences, and maintain credibility.

In this digital age, multi-platform content distribution is crucial. Museums can diversify their content formats by creating an array of media such as film and video contentimportance in newsaudience engagementinteractive contentarticles, videos, infographics, podcasts, and live streams. This ensures the museum’s messages reach audiences who have preferences for different formats, enhancing engagement and broadening reach. Utilizing social media platforms like Facebook, X (formerly Twitter), Instagram, LinkedIn, and TikTok allows museums to tailor their messaging to the unique audiences and features of each platform, maximizing their outreach potential. Moreover, submitting museum content to news aggregators like Google News and Apple News can increase visibility and reach a broader audience by tapping into platforms that many digital news consumers frequent.

Effective PR also involves real-time engagement and interaction. Maintaining an active social media presence is critical for museums; by regularly posting updates, responding to comments, and engaging with followers, they can foster a strong online community. Social media management tools can help schedule posts and monitor interactions, ensuring constant communication. Hosting live events, Q&A sessions, and exhibition launches on platforms like Facebook Live and Instagram Live allows museums to interact with their audience in real time, creating a sense of immediacy and connection. Collaborating with influencers and micro-influencers aligned with a museum’s brand values can elevate the institution’s message, helping to reach niche audiences who engage with these thought leaders.

Personalized and targeted campaigns are another pillar of effective PR strategies. Using data analytics to segment the audience based on demographics, interests, and behavior allows museums to tailor their messaging to resonate with each specific group. Creating personalized content that addresses the unique needs and interests of these segments enhances engagement, which can be further strengthened through email marketing and personalized social media ads. Retargeting campaigns can also be employed to re-engage users who have previously interacted with a museum’s content or website, reinforcing messages and driving conversions.

Building and maintaining credibility remains a constant priority. Museums should ensure all shared information is accurate and verifiable, with transparency about sources and context to avoid misinformation. Positioning the museum as a thought leader by contributing expert opinions and insights to reputable platforms can significantly bolster the institution’s authority and public trust. Providing media training for museum spokespeople ensures they can communicate the museum’s messages effectively and navigate interviews with confidence.authenticityethical storytellingMonitoring and analytics are also vital for assessing PR effectiveness. Social listening tools enable museums to monitor conversations about their institution, the broader museum sector, and peer institutions, keeping them informed about public sentiment and trends. Tracking key performance metrics—such as engagement rates, reach, impressions, and sentiment analysis—provides insights for refining strategies and improving future campaigns. Developing a crisis management plan that includes monitoring for potential issues, quick responses to negative coverage, and transparent communication with stakeholders ensures readiness in maintaining museum integrity.

Leveraging multimedia and interactive content enriches audience engagement. Museums can invest in high-quality video production for tutorials, behind-the-scenes footage, and visitor testimonials, sharing these on platforms like YouTube and TikTok. Creating interactive content such as polls, quizzes, and surveys engages audiences while gathering valuable feedback, using features like Instagram Stories and Twitter polls to facilitate such interactions. Visual storytelling through infographics, slideshows, and images conveys complex museum information in a digestible format, enhancing understanding and shareability.

Collaborating with digital media outlets further extends a museum’s influence. Building relationships with digital journalists and bloggers who cover arts and culture allows for tailored pitches and increases the likelihood of coverage. Contributing guest posts to renowned blogs and online publications showcases museum expertise to new audiences. Sponsored content on digital platforms offers another avenue for reaching targeted audiences and maintaining control over editorial direction.

Enhancing mobile accessibility ensures that museum content reaches users on the go. Ensuring content is optimized for mobile devices by using responsive web designs, crafting mobile-friendly emails, and producing vertical videos for platforms like Instagram fosters easy access. Using push notifications alerts audiences about important updates and events, helping drive traffic and engagement.

Emphasizing ethical practices is essential for upholding the museum’s reputation. Transparency and authenticity in all communications build trust, while highlighting corporate social responsibility initiatives and community involvement enhances the museum’s standing. Ethical storytelling ensures transparencyethical communicationtacticsbest for all reportersthat all narratives respect individuals and communities involved, embodying the museum’s commitment to inclusive and responsible representation.

By implementing these strategies, museum PR professionals can effectively navigate the shifting landscape of news consumption. They can engage diverse audiences across digital platforms while maintaining credibility, enhancing museum visibility, and building resilient stakeholder relationships endowed for long-term success.

info.title: Effective PR Tactics to Use with All Types of Reporters

listitem.para: Build Relationships: Establish and maintain strong relationships with reporters. Regularly engage with them through social media, emails, and phone calls.
Understand Their Beat: Know the specific topics and areas that the reporter covers. Tailor your pitches to align with their interests and beat.
Craft Compelling Pitches: Create concise, newsworthy, and relevant pitches. Highlight the unique angle or value of your story.
Provide Exclusive Content: Offer exclusive stories or information to specific reporters to build trust and increase the likelihood of coverage.
Be Timely: Pitch your stories at the right time. Be aware of deadlines and the news cycle to ensure your story is relevant and timely.
Offer Expert Sources: Provide access to knowledgeable and credible sources who can offer valuable insights and quotes for the reporter’s story.
Follow-Up: Politely follow up on your pitches without being overly persistent. Respect the reporter’s time and workload.
Provide High-Quality Materials: Supply well-written press releases, high-resolution images, and other supporting materials that can make the reporter’s job easier.
Be Transparent and Honest: Always provide accurate information and be upfront about any potential issues or limitations.journalist relationsbuilding trustbroadcast mediatelevision news distinctions
Monitor and Respond: Keep track of the reporter’s work and respond promptly to any inquiries or requests for additional information.

info.title: Differences between Television, Print, and Radio News

section.para: Television, print, and radio news are three distinct mediums through which news is delivered to the public. Each medium has its unique characteristics, strengths, and limitations, which influence how news is reported, consumed, and perceived. Understanding these differences is crucial for effectively engaging with each medium and tailoring your communication strategies accordingly. Here’s an in-depth look at the differences between television, print, and radio news.

Television news combines visual and audio elements, making it a highly engaging and dynamic medium. It uses video footage, graphics, and sound to convey information. Television news can have an immediate impact due to its visual nature, quickly capturing the audience’s attention and evoking emotions through imagery and sound. News segments on television are typically brief, often lasting as little as 30 seconds, which requires concise and impactful storytelling. Television news often includes live reporting from the scene of events, providing real-time updates and a sense of immediacy. The combination of visuals and audio makes television news highly engaging and memorable, and visuals and sound can evoke strong emotional responses, making stories more impactful. Television has a wide reach, with the potential to reach large and diverse audiences. However, the brevity of news segments can limit the depth of coverage and analysis, and producing television news requires significant resources, including equipment, personnel, and studio space. For example, a breaking news story about a natural disaster might include live footage from the scene, interviews with eyewitnesses, and expert commentary, providing a comprehensive and immediate overview of the event.

Print news is primarily text-based, with the addition of photographs and infographics to complement the written content. Print news (which often first appears on digital channels like websites) allows for more in-depth coverage and analysis of stories, providing detailed background information, context, and multiple perspectives. Print news creates a permanent record television newsbest PR tacticstacticsbest for televisionmedia relations tacticspress conferencesof events, which can be referenced and archived for future use. Print news is typically published on a regular schedule, such as daily, weekly, or monthly, depending on the publication. Print news can provide comprehensive coverage and in-depth analysis, offering readers a deeper understanding of issues. Established print publications often have a reputation for credibility and thorough reporting. Print news can be easily carried and read at the reader’s convenience. However, print news may not be as immediate as television or radio news, especially for breaking stories, and the rise of digital media has led to declining circulation and readership for traditional print publications. For example, a feature article in a newspaper about climate change might include detailed explanations of scientific research, interviews with experts, and an analysis of policy implications, providing readers with a comprehensive understanding of the issue.

Radio news is delivered through audio, relying on spoken words, sound bites, and music to convey information. Radio news can be updated quickly and frequently, making it an effective medium for breaking news and real-time updates. Radio is a highly portable medium, accessible in cars, homes, and workplaces, allowing listeners to stay informed while on the go. Radio news often uses storytelling techniques, with reporters painting vivid pictures through descriptive language and sound effects. Radio news can provide real-time updates and live coverage of events. Radio is accessible to a wide audience, including those who may not have access to television or the internet. The use of sound and storytelling can create an intimate and engaging listening experience. However, the absence of visual elements can limit the ability to convey certain types of information, and radio news segments are often brief, requiring concise and clear communication. For example, a radio news report on a political rally might include live audio from the event, interviews with attendees, and analysis from political commentators, providing listeners with a vivid and immediate sense of the event.

info.title: Best PR Tactics to Use with Television Reporters

section.para: Television remains one of the most powerful and influential media platforms, capable of reaching large and diverse audiences. Working effectively with television reporters requires a strategic approach that leverages the unique characteristics of the medium. Here are some of the best PR tactics to use when engaging with television reporters to secure positive coverage and maximize your message’s impact.press conferencesusage and planningTelevision is a visual medium, and compelling visuals are essential for capturing the audience’s attention and conveying your message effectively. Look for aspects of your story that can be visually compelling, such as events, demonstrations, or behind-the-scenes footage. Offer high-quality B-roll footage that television reporters can use to supplement their coverage, including video clips of your facilities, products, or events. Incorporate visual aids such as charts, infographics, and props during interviews or press conferences to enhance the visual appeal of your message. For example, if you are launching a new product, arrange a demonstration that showcases the product in action and provide B-roll footage of the product being used in real-life scenarios to give reporters engaging visuals to work with.

Television news segments are typically brief, so it’s crucial to communicate your key messages clearly and concisely. Develop concise and impactful soundbites that encapsulate your key messages, making them easy for reporters to use in their segments. During interviews, stay focused on your key messages and avoid going off on tangents. Practice delivering your messages succinctly and use simple, straightforward language that is easy for the general audience to understand. For instance, if you are promoting a new health initiative, prepare soundbites that highlight the key benefits and impact of the initiative, such as “Our program provides free health screenings to underserved communities, helping to detect and prevent serious illnesses.”

Building strong relationships with television reporters can increase the likelihood of securing positive coverage and establishing trust. Identify television reporters and producers who cover your industry or beat, and understand their interests, reporting style, and recent stories. Tailor your pitches to the specific interests and preferences of each reporter, highlighting why your story is relevant to their audience. Keep in touch with reporters through regular updates, press releases, and invitations to events, and be responsive and available for follow-up questions. For example, if you are in the tech industry, identify reporters who cover technology and innovation and send personalized pitches that highlight the unique aspects of your story and why it would be of interest to their viewers.

Press conferences and media events provide an opportunity to deliver your message directly to television reporters and create engaging visuals. Choose a location that is visually appealing and relevant to your story, and ensure that the venue is equipped with the necessary audiovisual equipment. Send invitations to key television reporters and media outlets well in advance, and provide them with a media kit that includes background information, press releases, and visual assets. Train your spokespeople to deliver key messages confidently and handle media questions effectively, ensuring they are prepared with soundbites and talking points. For example, if you are announcing a major milestone, organize a press conference at your museum, set up a visually appealing backdrop, provide B-roll footage, and prepare your CEO to deliver a compelling speech and answer questions from reporters.interviewsradio story pitchinginterviewsmedia spokesperson preparationexpert commentaryinterviews preparation

Offering exclusive stories or embargoed information can generate interest and build goodwill with television reporters. Provide exclusive access to a significant story, interview, or event to a specific television reporter or outlet, increasing the likelihood of in-depth coverage. Share information with reporters under embargo, allowing them to prepare their coverage in advance, leading to more comprehensive and accurate reporting. Ensure that the timing of the exclusive or embargoed information aligns with your communication strategy and media outreach plan. For example, if you are launching a new educational program or exhibit, offer an exclusive first look to a prominent television reporter, providing them with access to interviews with key executives and behind-the-scenes footage, ensuring they have all the materials needed for a compelling story.

On-camera interviews are a key component of television news coverage. Being well-prepared can help you deliver your message effectively and make a positive impression. Rehearse your key messages and soundbites, practice speaking clearly and confidently, and maintain eye contact with the interviewer. Choose attire that is professional and camera-friendly, avoiding busy patterns and overly bright colors that can be distracting on camera. Remain calm and composed during the interview, even if faced with challenging questions, and take a moment to collect your thoughts before responding. For example, if you are the spokesperson for a nonprofit organization, practice delivering your key messages about your latest campaign, dress in professional attire, and maintain a calm and confident demeanor during the interview.

Monitoring and evaluating media coverage helps you understand the impact of your PR efforts and identify areas for improvement. Use media monitoring tools to track television coverage of your story, analyzing the tone, reach, and key messages conveyed in the coverage. Collect feedback from reporters and viewers to understand their perceptions and any areas for improvement. Use tacticsbest for radiopublic service announcements (PSAs)radio campaign toolthe insights gained from monitoring and feedback to refine your PR strategy and improve future media engagements. For example, after a major product launch, use media monitoring tools to track television coverage, analyze the coverage to see how well your key messages were conveyed, and gather feedback from reporters to identify any areas for improvement.

info.title: Best PR Tactics to Use with Radio Reporters

section.para: Radio remains a powerful medium for reaching diverse audiences, offering immediacy, portability, and a personal touch through the spoken word. Working effectively with radio reporters requires a strategic approach that leverages the unique characteristics of radio. Here are some of the best PR tactics to use when engaging with radio reporters to secure positive coverage and maximize your message’s impact.

Radio segments are often brief, so it’s crucial to communicate your key messages clearly and concisely. Listeners need to grasp your main points quickly. Prepare short, impactful soundbites that encapsulate your key messages, making them easy for reporters to use in their segments. Avoid jargon and technical terms, using straightforward language that is easy for the general audience to understand. During interviews, stay focused on your key messages and avoid going off on tangents. Practice delivering your messages succinctly. For example, if you are promoting a new community health initiative, prepare soundbites like, “Our program offers free health screenings to ensure everyone has access to essential healthcare services.”

Building strong relationships with radio reporters can increase the likelihood of securing positive coverage and establishing trust. Identify radio reporters who cover your industry or beat, and understand their interests, reporting style, and recent stories. Tailor your pitches to the specific interests and preferences of each reporter, highlighting why your story is relevant to their audience. Keep in touch with reporters through regular updates, press releases, and invitations to events, and be responsive and available for follow-up questions. For example, if you are pitching an education story, identify reporters who cover education and community issues. Send personalized pitches that highlight the unique aspects of your story and why it would be of interest to their listeners.

Radio is an audio-only medium, so providing high-quality audio clips and soundbites can enhance your chances of getting coverage. Record clear and professional soundbites that convey your key messages, ensuring the audio quality is high and free from background noise. Provide additional audio clips that reporters can use to supplement their coverage, such as interviews, event recordings, or ambient sounds. Choose spokespeople with engaging and articulate voices to deliver your soundbites, as a compelling voice can make your message more impactful. For example, if you are announcing a new environmental initiative, record soundbites from your CEO explaining the initiative’s goals and impact. Provide additional audio clips of interviews with community members and environmental experts.

Radio interviews and segments provide an opportunity to deliver your message directly to the audience. Being well-prepared can help you make a positive impression. Train your spokespeople to deliver key messages confidently and handle media questions effectively, ensuring they are prepared with soundbites and talking points. Coordinate with radio reporters to schedule interviews at convenient times, providing background information and context to help them prepare. Rehearse your key messages and sound bites, practicing speaking clearly and confidently while maintaining a conversational tone. For example, if you are the spokesperson for a nonprofit organization, practice delivering your key messages about your latest campaign. Schedule interviews with radio stations that have a strong community focus and provide reporters with background information about your organization.

Public service announcements (PSAs) are a valuable tool for promoting community initiatives, events, and public awareness campaigns on radio. Develop short, engaging PSAs that convey your key messages and call to action, ensuring the audio quality is high and the message is clear. Submit your PSAs to radio stations that align with your target audience, following each station’s guidelines for PSA submissions. Track when and where your PSAs are aired, using this information to evaluate the reach and impact of your campaign. For example, if you are organizing a community health fair, create a PSA that highlights the event’s date, location, and available services. Submit the PSA to local radio stations and monitor its airplay to gauge its effectiveness.

Offering exclusive stories or interviews can generate interest and build goodwill with radio reporters. Provide exclusive access to a significant story, interview, or event to a specific radio reporter or station, increasing the likelihood of in-depth coverage. Ensure that the timing of the exclusive media landscapemedia outlet differencesdigital mediadifferences from printinformation aligns with your communication strategy and media outreach plan. After the exclusive story or interview airs, follow up with the reporter to express appreciation and discuss potential future collaborations. For example, if you are launching a new product, offer an exclusive first interview with your CEO to a prominent radio station. Provide them with all the necessary information and materials to create a compelling segment.

Community and local radio stations often have strong connections with their audiences and can be valuable partners for promoting local initiatives and events. Research community and local radio stations that align with your target audience and geographic area. Establish relationships with local radio reporters and station managers by attending community events and engaging with local media to build rapport. Use local radio to promote community initiatives, events, and partnerships, highlighting the local impact and relevance of your story. For example, if you are a local business sponsoring a community event, work with local radio stations to promote the event. Offer interviews with event organizers and provide audio clips that highlight the event’s significance to the community.

Monitoring and evaluating radio coverage helps you understand the impact of your PR efforts and identify areas for improvement. Use media monitoring tools to track radio coverage of your story, analyzing the tone, reach, and key messages conveyed in the coverage. Collect feedback from reporters and listeners to understand their perceptions and any areas for improvement. Use the insights gained from monitoring and feedback to refine your PR strategy and improve future media engagements. For example, after a major campaign, use media monitoring tools to track radio coverage. Analyze the coverage to see how well your key messages were conveyed and gather feedback from reporters to identify any areas for improvement.

info.title: Key Distinctions between Print and Digital Media

section.para: The differences between traditional print news and digital media are significant and impact how PR professionals approach each medium.

listitem.para: Format: Physical newspapers and magazines.
Publication Frequency: Often daily, weekly, or monthly.
Distribution: Limited to geographic areas where the publication is circulated.
Space Constraints: Limited space for articles, leading to more selective content.
Permanence: Once printed, content cannot be changed or updated.
Audience Engagement: Limited to letters to the editor or in-person events.
Credibility: Often perceived as more credible due to established reputations and rigorous editorial standards.
Lead Time: Longer lead times for stories due to the printing process.
Revenue Model: Primarily through subscriptions and advertising.
Format: Online articles, blogs, social media posts, videos, podcasts, and so on.
Publication Frequency: Continuous, with the ability to publish updates in real time.
Distribution: Global reach, accessible to anyone with an internet connection.
Space Constraints: Virtually unlimited space, allowing for more in-depth coverage and multimedia elements.
Permanence: Content can be updated, corrected, or removed at any time.
Audience Engagement: High levels of interaction through comments, shares, likes, and direct messages.
Credibility: Varies widely; some digital outlets are highly reputable, while others may lack editorial oversight.
Lead Time: Shorter lead times, allowing for rapid response to breaking news.television newsreporter rolesjournalist relationsbuilding trustask the expertLisa Stark
Revenue Model: Diverse, including advertising, subscriptions, sponsored content, and donations.
Pitching: Tailor pitches to fit the format and constraints of each medium. For print, focus on concise, high-impact stories. For digital, consider multimedia elements and timely updates.
Engagement: Utilize social media and other digital platforms to engage with audiences and reporters in real time.
Content Creation: Develop a mix of content types (articles, videos, infographics) to suit different digital platforms.
Monitoring: Use digital tools to track coverage and audience engagement more effectively.
Credibility Management: Be mindful of the varying credibility levels of digital outlets and choose where to place stories accordingly.
Understanding these differences helps PR professionals craft more effective strategies for each medium, ensuring their messages reach the intended audience in the most impactful way.

section.para: Interview with Lisa Stark, an award-winning television network news correspondent and veteran broadcast journalist. Stark was a national correspondent for ABC News for two decades. She then worked as a correspondent for Al Jazeera America, followed by Education Week and the PBS NewsHour. Stark then served as the Assistant Vice President for Communications and Media at American University.

para.emphasis: Q: As a communicator, what are the best ways to start networking with TV news reporters?

section.para: Communicators should try to build relationships with reporters before they have news to pitch. Follow reporters on social media and encourage them to follow you. Comment on and share their stories. If they do a story in your area of expertise, reach out and let them know your thoughts and that you would be available for a future story, or suggest a follow-up. You can also offer journalist relationsbuilding trustreporters a chance to get video B-roll, especially of something they might not otherwise have access to.

para.emphasis: Question: It doesn’t seem like TV reporters have “beats” like they used to in the past. How do I find the best reporter for the story?

section.para: Network reporters often have beats, but that is not always the case at the local level. To figure out which reporter is best for your story, keep an eye on the type of news the reporters are covering. Also, get to know the assignment editor at a local TV station. When you have news to share, contact them and see which reporter they would suggest for the story.

para.emphasis: Question: What does the TV news producer do versus the TV reporter?

section.para: The TV news producer is a critical part of the reporting team. Producers exist primarily at the network level, less so in local news. The producer will help gather editorial information and find people to interview. The producer may even conduct some of the interviews if the correspondent is busy. In some cases, they will help write the story. It is critical for communicators to get to know the producer. That person might be easier to reach than the correspondent if you have news to share.

para.emphasis: Question: Who is the assignment editor?

section.para: In a television newsroom, think of the assignment editor like a dispatcher. The editor will send out crews and reporters on breaking news, may decide which breaking news story to launch on, and will keep details of upcoming news events that the station may want to cover. The assignment editor is not always the person to decide on news coverage but can be a good first point of contact.

para.emphasis: Question: Are there any differences between how a local reporter approaches a story versus a national news reporter? Are they interested in different stories?

section.para: Local reporters may be working on numerous stories on the same day, so they don’t often have the luxury of going in depth on a topic, as a national news reporter might. They both would approach a story looking for good interviews, good visuals, and a compelling narrative. The focus of a local versus a national story is also different—for obvious reasons. A local story has interest to a local audience—anything from a deadly local accident to a local scandal, to the success of the local high school football team. A national reporter is looking for a story with more widespread interest and focus, or one that contains a universal truth. All reporters, though, are interested in human interest stories, the so-called “people stories,” that resonate with many viewers.

para.emphasis: Question: Tell us more about your “silver platter” metaphor and how communicators can help reporters with their stories?

section.para: Reporters are busy and have tight deadlines, and it can help your chances of getting your story told if you do some of the groundwork for them. I’m not suggesting you serve everything up on a silver platter, but it helps to have some ingredients in place. When you’re pitching a story, create a narrative. Make the pitch newsy, or the reporter will put it aside. Offer visuals, perhaps handout footage or photos, or access to filming the pictures that the story needs. Reporters always want the human interest element, so if you can suggest “real people” to interview, that will help too.

para.emphasis: Question: Is the relationship between PR person and reporter always antagonistic, or is that a myth?

section.para: As an ABC News network news correspondent, I had close, productive relationships with many PR professionals. We had mutual trust and respect and understood each other’s roles. That doesn’t mean I wrote the story as they wanted it, or even in a favorable way. It does mean that we treated each other fairly. The truth is PR professionals need reporters, and reporters need PR professionals.

para.emphasis: Question: How do I make sure my museum or leadership gets treated fairly by the media?

section.para: The first key to fair treatment is to build a relationship with a reporter based on trust and respect. That said, you will not be able to control the content of the story, and it may not end up being the story that you had hoped to tell. Do a little homework on the reporter who comes calling, and make sure you feel their work is reputable and that you are likely to get a fair shake.

para.emphasis: Question: If a reporter is calling about a negative story, should I respond?

section.para: Always respond to a reporter’s phone call. It does not mean that you must agree to an interview, but it’s good practice to respond and either agree or decline to speak with them. That way, they may be more likely to come calling when there is a positive story to report.

para.emphasis: Questions: Should I even bother working with TV news since the stories are so short?

section.para: TV shows still get a lot of eyeballs. ABC News World News is the highest-rated network news show and has over 8 million viewers a night. So, one story can have a lot of reach, and you can repost it on your website and social media for a larger impact.

listitem.para: In the competitive media landscape, it’s crucial for public relations (PR) professionals to craft news pitches that are concise, relevant, and engaging to capture journalists’ attention. This involves highlighting the newsworthiness of a story while understanding and aligning with a journalist’s interests and audience, which is particularly relevant for museums seeking coverage of their exhibits and events.

A well-designed news pitch serves as more than just a tool to secure media coverage; it is an opportunity to establish lasting relationships with journalists. By providing valuable information that aligns with a journalist’s beat, museum PR professionals can position themselves as reliable sources, facilitating long-term media engagement and future success in media pitching.

Securing media coverage through an effective news pitch can significantly amplify a museum’s message, reaching wider audiences and enhancing its public reputation. This increased exposure not only generates buzz around exhibitions or events but also lends credibility and authority to the museum’s initiatives and missions.

chapter.para: In the vibrant landscape of media relations and communications within the museum field, honing the craft of a compelling news pitch is essential for PR professionals. A well-crafted pitch draws journalists’ attention, secures media coverage, and amplifies a museum’s narrative to diverse audiences. Given the sheer volume of pitches journalists receive daily, standing out requires strategic foresight, creativity, and a deep understanding of newsworthiness.

This guide is specifically designed for professionals in the museum sector, aiding them in developing and delivering news pitches that engage media outlets. Whether publicizing a groundbreaking exhibit at a science museum, announcing a pivotal historical exhibit, or sharing insights from art curators, a strategic pitch can transform an overlooked email into a headline feature.news pitchingcrafting effective pitchesAccording to a recent Cision 2024 report,
“How to Write a PR Pitch that Gets Results: 7 Journalist-Approved Tips” | Cision. creating an effective PR pitch begins with identifying a relevant, newsworthy angle. For your pitch to capture attention, it must provide a fresh, compelling perspective that resonates with the journalist’s readership. Consider the current relevance of your museum’s story, its connection to ongoing cultural events or trends, and its uniqueness compared to previously covered topics. Begin your pitch with a compelling justification for why a journalist should explore your story, going beyond simply announcing a new exhibit or museum milestone by linking it to broader cultural or scientific conversations.

An engaging subject line is crucial, as most journalists prefer email pitches. Yet, many receive more than one hundred email pitches weekly. Your subject line should be both eye-catching and informative, succinctly conveying the crux of your museum-related PR pitch.
