Avoid gimmicky tactics and marketing jargon likely to lead to instant deletion. Keep the subject line concise—ideally under ten words—and to the point. Use brackets to highlight the topic, sparking curiosity about its significance.

Once you’ve captured attention with a strong subject line, maintain it with a skimmable pitch. Overwhelmed journalists appreciate pitches that are easy to skim, allowing them to absorb the facts quickly. Use short paragraphs bolstered by bullet points to outline key aspects of your museum story. Address the essential who, what, when, where, and why succinctly. Provide ample details for journalists to assess their interests and invite them to reach out for more information. Finish with a clear call to action, simplifying the next step if they are engaged.

Including multimedia in your pitch can significantly aid journalists. Fifty-five percent of journalists are more likely to pursue a pitch with multimedia. Tailor the multimedia to suit the format you are targeting; for instance, a history museum might emphasize high-quality photos of artifacts, while a science museum might use infographics explaining exhibit content.

Offering expert interviews, perhaps with a celebrated historian or art curator, can enhance credibility and attract journalists. Value is placed on pitches that provide access to experts, and PR professionals should ensure these subjects are readily available and well-prepared for interview requests. Journalists expect professionalism and dependability in fulfilling promises made in pitches.Incorporating data can be an effective way to capture attention. Journalists value original research, such as visitor insights, exhibit popularity metrics, and public interest surveys related to museum topics. The State of the Media report highlights this as highly sought-after content. Data enriches your museum story and lends credibility, which is crucial for journalists.

Investing in a robust media database can revolutionize your ability to create impactful pitches that draw journalist interest and achieve earned media. Such a database can help identify journalists interested in museum stories, understand their coverage history, and preferred pitch styles. Tools like CisionOne Outreach streamline the process of identifying relevant media contacts and provide reliable contact data for countless media professionals. This data supports pitch personalization, including recent published content and areas of interest, enhancing efficiency and accuracy in media relations.

As emphasized by Muck Rack, successful pitch crafting requires a strategic, personalized approach. The days of mass emailing are gone; journalists easily recognize untargeted pitches, which can jeopardize relationship building. Always personalize your pitch by using the journalist’s name and referencing a recent article they’ve written, particularly about museums or related fields. This effort is often rewarded with positive feedback.

Conciseness is vital, as journalists have limited time for lengthy emails. Aim for two to three concise paragraphs in your initial communication. Ensure your news is truly newsworthy; journalists do not appreciate unsubstantial pitches and may critique them publicly. Allow journalists time to review your pitch before following up. Silence after a follow-up generally indicates a lack of interest.

Avoid cold-calling journalists; most prefer not to receive pitches via phone. If necessary, confirm it’s a suitable time before proceeding. Similarly, pitching on social media is typically discouraged unless the journalist explicitly welcomes it on their profile or you have an established rapport. Avoid simultaneously pitching multiple journalists in public forums like Twitter, as identical messages are easily detected.

After securing successful coverage, thank the journalist and share the publication across platforms like X (formerlyTwitter), Facebook, LinkedIn, and through email. This helps amplify the story’s reach and shows appreciation, strengthening relationships with journalists in the museum sector.news pitchingpitch personalization importancenews pitchingelements of a strong pitchmedia relations tacticspersonalized pitchesmedia relationspitch personalizationjournalist relationspitch personalization

info.title: The Importance of a Strong News Pitch

section.para: Journalists are inundated with pitches, press releases, and story ideas every day. To capture their attention, a news pitch must be concise, relevant, and engaging. A strong pitch not only highlights the newsworthiness of the story but also demonstrates an understanding of the journalist’s interests and audience. By crafting a pitch that stands out, PR professionals can increase the likelihood of their story being covered.

A well-crafted news pitch is more than just a tool for securing coverage; it is also an opportunity to build and strengthen relationships with journalists. By providing valuable and relevant information, PR professionals can establish themselves as reliable sources and foster long-term relationships with the media. These relationships are crucial for ongoing media engagement and future pitching success.

Securing media coverage through a strong news pitch can significantly amplify an organization’s message. Media coverage not only reaches a wider audience but also lends credibility and authority to the information being shared. A successful pitch can generate buzz, drive public interest, and enhance the organization’s reputation.

info.title: Key Specific Elements of a Strong News Pitch

section.para: The foundation of a strong news pitch is newsworthiness. To determine if a story is newsworthy, PR professionals should consider factors such as timeliness, significance, proximity, prominence, human interest, and novelty. A newsworthy pitch addresses current events, impacts a large audience, involves notable individuals or organizations, evokes emotions, or offers something unique and unexpected.

A successful news pitch is tailored to the specific interests and needs of the journalist and their audience. PR professionals should research the journalist’s previous work, the media outlet’s focus, and the preferences of their target audience. By aligning the pitch with the journalist’s beat and the outlet’s editorial style, PR professionals can increase the chances of their story being picked up.

Journalists are often pressed for time, so a news pitch must be clear, concise, and to the point. The pitch should quickly convey the key message, highlight the newsworthy elements, and provide essential details. Avoiding jargon and overly technical language ensures that the pitch is easily understood and accessible.

The subject line of an email pitch is the first thing a journalist sees, and it plays a crucial role in determining whether the pitch will be opened. An engaging subject line should be attention-grabbing, informative, and relevant to the story. It should entice the journalist to read further and learn more about the pitch.

The opening of the pitch should include a compelling hook that captures the journalist’s interest. This could be a surprising fact, a provocative question, or a powerful quote. The hook sets the tone for the pitch and encourages the journalist to continue reading.

While the pitch should be concise, it should also provide enough supporting information to give the journalist a clear understanding of the story. This includes key details, relevant statistics, quotes from credible sources, and any additional context that enhances the newsworthiness of the pitch. Providing links to press releases, background materials, and multimedia assets can also be helpful.

A strong news pitch includes a clear call to action, guiding the journalist on the next steps. This could be an invitation to an event, an offer for an interview with a spokesperson, or a request for coverage. Providing contact information and making it easy for the journalist to follow up is essential.

info.title: Steps to Developing a Strong News Pitch

listitem.para: Identify the Story

Begin by identifying a newsworthy story that aligns with your organization’s goals and the interests of the media. Consider the key elements of newsworthiness and determine what makes the story relevant and compelling.
Research the Journalist and Media Outlet

Conduct thorough research on the journalist and the media outlet you are pitching to. Understand their beat, audience, and previous work. Tailor your pitch to align with their interests and the outlet’s editorial style.
Craft the Pitch

Write a clear, concise, and engaging pitch that includes an attention-grabbing subject line, a compelling hook, and essential details. Highlight the newsworthy elements and provide supporting information. Ensure that the pitch is free of jargon and easily understood.
Personalize the Pitch

Personalize the pitch by addressing the journalist by name and referencing their previous work or interests. Demonstrating that you have done your homework and understand their focus can increase the chances of your pitch being considered.
Include a Call to Action

Clearly state what you want the journalist to do next, whether it’s attending an event, conducting an interview, or covering the story.news pitchingsocial media pitchingnews pitchingphone pitchingnews pitchingemail pitchingProvide contact information and make it easy for the journalist to follow up.
Follow-Up

If you don’t receive a response within a reasonable time frame, consider sending a polite follow-up email. Reiterate the key points of your pitch and express your willingness to provide additional information or answer any questions.

section.para: Email is the most common method for delivering news pitches. Ensure that your email is well-formatted, with a clear subject line, concise body text, and relevant attachments or links. Avoid sending large files that may clog the journalist’s inbox.

In some cases, a phone or text pitch may be appropriate, especially if you have an existing relationship with the journalist. Be respectful of the journalist’s time, and have a clear and concise script prepared. Offer to send additional information via email if needed.

Social media platforms, such as X (formerly Twitter) and LinkedIn, can also be used for pitching, especially for building initial connections with journalists. Keep social media pitches brief and direct, and follow up with more detailed information via email if the journalist expresses interest.

info.title: Differences between Good Pitches and Bad Pitches

section.para: Crafting a compelling news pitch is an art that requires a deep understanding of what journalists are looking for and how to present information in a way that captures their attention. The difference between a good pitch and a bad pitch can determine whether your story gets covered or ignored. Here, we explore the key differences between good pitches and bad pitches, providing examples to illustrate these distinctions.

info.title: Key Differences between Good Pitches and Bad Pitches

section.para: A good pitch is tailored to the specific interests and needs of the journalist and their audience. It demonstrates that the PR professional has done their homework and understands what the journalist is looking for.
Subject: Exclusive Interview Opportunity with Renowned Climate Scientist Dr. Jane Smith
Hi [Journalist’s Name],

I hope this email finds you well. I recently read your insightful article on the impact of climate change on coastal communities and thought you might be interested in an exclusive interview opportunity with Dr. Jane Smith, a leading climate scientist. Dr. Smith has just published a groundbreaking study on the effects of rising sea levels and is available for interviews next week.
Please let me know if you would like to schedule an interview or need any additional information.
Best regards,
[Your Name]
A bad pitch is generic and lacks personalization. It is often sent to multiple journalists without considering their specific interests or beats.

I wanted to share some exciting news about a new study conducted by XYZ University that reveals the surprising benefits of urban green spaces on mental health. The study found that spending just twenty minutes in a park can significantly reduce stress levels and improve overall well-being.
The lead researcher, Dr. Emily Brown, is available for interviews to discuss the findings and their implications for urban planning. I have attached a summary of the study for your reference.
Best regards,

A bad pitch is often lengthy, unclear, and filled with jargon. It fails to quickly convey the key message, making it difficult for the journalist to understand the story’s relevance.

info.title: Tips for Crafting Effective Pitch Subject Lines

section.para: The subject line of your pitch email is the first thing a journalist sees, and it plays a crucial role in determining whether your email will be opened or ignored. A compelling subject line can capture the journalist’s attention and entice them to read further, while a weak or generic subject line can result in your pitch being overlooked. Here are some tips for crafting effective pitch subject lines, along with examples to illustrate each tip.
Tip:
Keep your subject line clear and to the point. Avoid using jargon or overly complex language. The journalist should be able to quickly understand the main idea of your pitch.
Example:
“Exclusive Preview: XYZ Museum’s New Ancient Civilizations Exhibit”
Tip:
Emphasize the newsworthy aspect of your pitch. Whether it’s a new product launch, a significant event, or a groundbreaking study, make sure the subject line conveys why the story is important.
Example:
“New Study Reveals Surprising Benefits of Urban Green Spaces”
Tip:
If your pitch is time-sensitive, create a sense of urgency in the subject line. This can encourage the journalist to open your email promptly.
Example:
“Last Chance to Cover: XYZ Museum’s Annual Art Gala This Weekend”
Tip:
Personalize the subject line to make it more relevant to the journalist. Mentioning their name, their beat, or a recent article they wrote can make your pitch stand out.
Example:
“[Journalist’s Name], Exclusive Interview Opportunity with Climate Scientist Dr. Jane Smith”
Tip:
Incorporate numbers or statistics to add specificity and make your subject line more compelling. This can help convey the significance of your story.
Example:
“85% of Consumers Seek Sustainable Fashion: New Survey Results”
Tip:
Pose a thought-provoking question that piques the journalist’s curiosity and encourages them to open your email to find the answer.
Example:
“Can Urban Green Spaces Really Reduce Stress? New Research Says Yes”
Tip:
If your pitch offers an exclusive or unique opportunity, such as an interview, behind-the-scenes access, or a first look, make sure to highlight this in the subject line.
Example:
“Exclusive Access: Behind the Scenes of XYZ Museum’s New Exhibit”
Tip:
Aim for a subject line that is 6–10 words long. Shorter subject lines are easier to read and are more likely to be fully visible in the journalist’s inbox.
Example:
“New Eco-Friendly Clothing Line Launch”
Tip:
Incorporate action words that convey excitement and urgency. Words like “discover,” “unveil,” “reveal,” and “explore” can make your subject line more dynamic.
Example:
“Discover the Future of Sustainable Fashion with XYZ Brand”
Tip:
If you have the opportunity, test different subject lines to see which ones perform best. Pay attention to open rates and responses to optimize your subject lines for future pitches.
Example:
“New Study on Urban Green Spaces” vs. “Urban Green Spaces: Surprising Health Benefits Revealed”

info.title: How Pitches Change When Targeting TV News, Radio, and Print Journalists

section.para: Crafting a successful pitch requires tailoring your message to the specific medium you are targeting. TV news, radio, and print journalism each have unique characteristics, audience expectations, and content formats. Understanding these differences is crucial for creating pitches that resonate with journalists and increase the likelihood of media coverage. Here’s how pitches change when targeting TV news, radio, and print journalists, along with examples for each medium.

When targeting TV news journalists, it is essential to focus on visual appeal, conciseness, and timeliness. TV news relies heavily on visuals, so stories with strong visual elements, such as compelling footage, interviews, and on-site coverage, are more likely to be picked up. TV segments are typically brief, so pitches need to be concise and to the point. Additionally, TV news often focuses on current events and breaking news, making timeliness crucial. Therefore, when crafting a pitch for TV news, highlight the visual aspects of the story, emphasize the timeliness and relevance of the news, and offer opportunities for on-site coverage or live interviews.
Example:
Subject: Exclusive Access: XYZ Museum’s “Treasures of Ancient Civilizations” Exhibit—Perfect for TV Coverage
Hi [Journalist’s Name],

I hope this message finds you well. I wanted to share an exciting opportunity for exclusive TV coverage of XYZ Museum’s upcoming exhibit, “Treasures of Ancient Civilizations,” opening on February 1, 2025.

This visually stunning exhibit features over 200 rare artifacts from ancient Egypt, Greece, and Mesopotamia, including a replica of the Rosetta Stone and the mummy of Ramses II. We have set up interactive displays and virtual reality experiences that bring the ancient world to life, making it perfect for captivating TV segments.

We invite you to join us for an exclusive preview and live broadcast opportunity. Dr. Emily Brown, the curator of the exhibit, will be available for on-camera interviews to provide insights into the artifacts and the stories behind them.
Please let me know if you would like to schedule a visit or need any additional information.
Best regards,
[Your Name]
Public Relations Manager
XYZ Museum

When targeting radio journalists, the focus shifts to audio quality, storytelling, and expert commentary. Radio relies on sound, so pitches should highlight the audio elements of the story, such as compelling interviews, sound bites, and ambient sounds. Storytelling is also important, as radio segments often involve in-depth discussions and narratives. Providing expert commentary or access to knowledgeable spokespeople can enhance the pitch’s appeal. Therefore, when crafting a pitch for radio, emphasize the audio quality, provide a compelling narrative, and offer expert commentary or interviews.
Example:
Subject: Interview Opportunity: Dr. Emily Brown Discusses XYZ Museum’s New Exhibit on Ancient Civilizations
Hi [Journalist’s Name],
I’m reaching out to share an exciting story for your listeners about XYZ Museum’s new exhibit, “Treasures of Ancient Civilizations,” opening on February 1, 2025.

This exhibit features over 200 rare artifacts from ancient Egypt, Greece, and Mesopotamia, and offers a fascinating journey through history. Dr. Emily Brown, the curator of the exhibit, is available for an in-depth radio interview to discuss the significance of these artifacts and the stories behind them.

Dr. Brown can provide engaging sound bites and expert insights that will captivate your audience. We believe this story will resonate with your listeners, especially those interested in history and culture.
Please let me know if you would like to schedule an interview or need any additional information.
Best regards,
[Your Name]
Public Relations Manager
XYZ Museum

When targeting print journalists, the emphasis is on detailed information, written content, and supporting materials. Print journalism allows for more in-depth coverage, so pitches should provide comprehensive information, including background details, statistics, and quotes. Written content should be well-crafted and engaging, capturing the journalist’s interest. Supporting materials, such as high-quality images, infographics, and press releases, can enhance the pitch’s effectiveness. Therefore, when crafting a pitch for print, provide detailed information, ensure the written content is engaging, and include supporting materials to strengthen the story.
Example:
Subject: In-Depth Feature: XYZ Museum’s “Treasures of Ancient Civilizations” Exhibit
Hi [Journalist’s Name],
I hope this email finds you well. I wanted to share an exciting story idea for an in-depth feature on XYZ Museum’s upcoming exhibit, “Treasures of Ancient Civilizations,” opening on February 1, 2025.

This exhibit showcases over 200 rare artifacts from ancient Egypt, Greece, and Mesopotamia, including a replica of the Rosetta Stone and the mummy of Ramses II. The exhibit also features interactive displays and virtual reality experiences that bring the ancient world to life.

Dr. Emily Brown, the curator of the exhibit, is available for interviews to provide detailed insights into the artifacts and the historical significance of the exhibit. We have high-resolution images and press materials available to support your coverage.

We believe this story will captivate your readers with its rich historical content and unique visual elements. Please let me know if you would like to schedule an interview with Dr. Brown or need any additional information.news pitchingpitch personalization importancenews pitchingcommon pitching mistakes (cardinal sins)media relations tacticspersonalized pitchesmedia relationspitch personalizationjournalist relationspitch personalization
Best regards,
[Your Name]
Public Relations Manager
XYZ Museum

Crafting and delivering a news pitch is a delicate art that requires careful consideration of the journalist’s needs, the newsworthiness of the story, and the clarity of the message. However, there are several common mistakes—often referred to as “cardinal sins”—that can derail even the most promising pitches. Avoiding these pitfalls is crucial for increasing the likelihood of your pitch being well-received and securing media coverage. Here are some cardinal sins of news pitching.

listitem.para: Sin: Sending generic, mass-distributed pitches that do not address the specific interests or beats of the journalist.

Why It’s a Problem: Journalists receive numerous pitches daily, and generic pitches are easily dismissed. Personalization shows that you have done your homework and understand the journalist’s focus and audience.
Example of a Bad Pitch: “Dear Journalist, We have an exciting new product launch. Please let us know if you are interested.”
How to Avoid: Research the journalist’s previous work, interests, and the media outlet’s audience. Tailor your pitch to align with their specific needs and preferences.

Example of a Good Pitch: “Hi [Journalist’s Name], I recently read your article on sustainable fashion and thought you might be interested in our new eco-friendly clothing line made from recycled materials. Would you like to learn more?”news pitchingpitch follow-up etiquette
Sin: Sending pitches that are too lengthy, filled with jargon, or overly complicated.
Why It’s a Problem: Journalists are often pressed for time and need to quickly understand the key points of a pitch. Long, complicated pitches can be overwhelming and are likely to be ignored.

Example of a Bad Pitch: “Dear Journalist, Our company has developed a revolutionary new product that leverages cutting-edge technology to optimize performance and efficiency. The product features a multi-layered architecture with advanced algorithms and state-of-the-art components.”
How to Avoid: Keep your pitch concise and to the point. Use clear, simple language and focus on the most important aspects of the story.

Example of a Good Pitch: “Hi [Journalist’s Name], We are excited to announce our new eco-friendly clothing line made from recycled materials. This innovative line reduces waste and promotes sustainability. Would you be interested in an exclusive preview?”
Sin: Pitching stories that lack newsworthiness or relevance to the journalist’s audience.

Why It’s a Problem: Journalists are looking for stories that are timely, significant, and relevant to their readers, viewers, or listeners. A pitch that lacks these elements is unlikely to be considered.
Example of a Bad Pitch: “Dear Journalist, Our company has a new logo. Please let us know if you would like to cover this story.”

How to Avoid: Evaluate the newsworthiness of your story by considering factors such as timeliness, significance, proximity, prominence, human interest, and novelty. Ensure that your pitch highlights these elements.

section.para: Example of a Good Pitch: “Hi [Journalist’s Name], We are thrilled to announce our new initiative to reduce plastic waste in our community. This program involves local schools and businesses and aims to recycle 10,000 pounds of plastic by the end of the year. Would you be interested in covering this impactful story?”follow-up to pitchmedia pitch etiquette

listitem.para: Sin: Not following up on your pitch or doing so inappropriately.
Why It’s a Problem: Journalists may miss your initial pitch due to their busy schedules. However, excessive or poorly timed follow-ups can be annoying and counterproductive.
Example of a Bad Follow-Up: “Dear Journalist, I sent you a pitch last week and haven’t heard back. Please let me know if you are interested.”
How to Avoid: Send a polite and timely follow-up email, typically within a week of the initial pitch. Reiterate the key points and express your willingness to provide additional information.

Example of a Good Follow-Up: “Hi [Journalist’s Name], I wanted to follow up on my previous email about our new eco-friendly clothing line. I believe this story would resonate with your readers interested in sustainable fashion. Please let me know if you need any additional information or would like to schedule an interview.”
Sin: Disregarding the journalist’s preferred method of communication or pitching stories that do not align with their beat.

Why It’s a Problem: Journalists have specific preferences for how they like to receive pitches and the types of stories they cover. Ignoring these preferences can result in your pitch being overlooked.
Example of a Bad Pitch: Sending a pitch about a tech product to a journalist who covers lifestyle and wellness.
How to Avoid: Research the journalist’s beat and preferred method of communication. Tailor your pitch to align with their interests and follow their preferred pitching guidelines.

Example of a Good Pitch: “Hi [Journalist’s Name], I noticed that you cover sustainable living and thought you might be interested in our new eco-friendly home products. These products are designed to reduce waste and promote a greener lifestyle. Would you like to learn more?”news pitchingexamples of pitches for exhibits, events, acquisitions, community projectsmuseum references and case studiesexhibit launches
Sin: Failing to provide sufficient supporting information, such as quotes, statistics, or multimedia assets.
Why It’s a Problem: Journalists need detailed information to develop their stories. A pitch that lacks supporting information may be seen as incomplete or unconvincing.
Example of a Bad Pitch: “Dear Journalist, We have a new product that we think you will find interesting. Please let us know if you would like to cover it.”
How to Avoid: Include relevant supporting information, such as quotes from key individuals, statistics, and links to press releases or multimedia assets.
Example of a Good Pitch:

section.para: Hi [Journalist’s Name], We are excited to announce our new eco-friendly clothing line made from recycled materials. This innovative line reduces waste and promotes sustainability. According to our recent survey, 85% of consumers are looking for more sustainable fashion options. Our CEO, Jane Doe, is available for interviews to discuss this initiative. Please find attached high-resolution images and a press release with additional details.

listitem.para: Sin: Being overly pushy or aggressive in your pitch or follow-up communications.

Why It’s a Problem: Journalists appreciate professionalism and respect for their time. Being pushy or aggressive can damage your relationship with the journalist and reduce the likelihood of coverage.
Example of a Bad Pitch: “Dear Journalist, You need to cover this story. It’s the best thing you’ll hear about all year. Please respond immediately.”
How to Avoid: Be polite, respectful, and professional in all communications. Express your enthusiasm for the story without being overbearing.

section.para: Example of a Good Pitch: “Hi [Journalist’s Name], I hope you’re doing well. I wanted to share an exciting story about our new eco-friendly clothing line made from recycled materials. We believe this initiative will resonate with your readers interested in sustainable fashion. Please let me know if you would like more information or to schedule an interview. Thank you for your consideration.”news pitchingtemplates for museum news pitchesmuseum references and case studiesspecial eventmuseum references and case studiesmajor acquisition announcement
