listitem.para: Museums must continuously adapt their media relations strategies to keep pace with the digital transformation of communication channels.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is revolutionizing museum media relations by enhancing media monitoring, sentiment analysis, and content creation. AI enables museums to predict trends, track media mentions, and create targeted content, allowing for precision in communications and the ability to swiftly respond to public sentiment.

Influencer marketing remains a powerful tool for museums in reaching new audiences and bolstering credibility, while multimedia formats, including video and augmented reality (AR), offer immersive experiences that captivate audiences, meaning museums must embrace these evolving formats to effectively engage the public in storytelling.

The role of public relations (PR) professionals as strategic advisers becomes increasingly crucial, ensuring that museum narratives are ethical, resonate with diverse communities, and align with broader institutional goals.
Employee internal communications is key to building a strong culture.

chapter.para: The future of PR for museums is set for a transformative shift, driven by rapid technological advancements, evolving audience behaviors, and the constantly changing media landscape. The digital age has redefined traditional paradigms, presenting both challenges and opportunities. As museums, like other cultural institutions, navigate this new terrain, they must adapt their PR strategies to thrive in this dynamic environment. Emerging technologies, such as AI, changes in media consumption, and evolving interaction strategies, are some of the forces shaping the future of media relations for museums.

Over recent decades, the media landscape has evolved dramatically, with digital media superseding traditional media outlets and leading to a decline in print circulation while propelling a shift toward online news consumption. Social media platforms, now key information sources, offer real-time updates and user-generated content, thus democratizing information flow and giving smaller museums a voice on par with larger entities. Consequently, museum PR professionals must adapt to a fragmented, fast-paced environment where journalists, influencers, and ordinary users operate on a level field. This requires museums to craft PR strategies that are agile, adaptable, and capable of engaging diverse audiences.

AI stands at the forefront of the future of museum media relations. AI tools are currently enhancing various aspects of PR, from media monitoring and sentiment analysis to innovative content creation and distribution methodologies. Museums can leverage AI to gain real-time insights, predict emerging trends, and tailor their communications with surgical precision. For instance, AI-backed media monitoring can track mentions of exhibitions or events across multiple platforms, analyze sentiment, and drive actionable insights to refine PR strategies. AI also assists in identifying key influencers and journalists, optimizing targeting, and generating personalized content that resonates with specific museum audience segments.

The integration of AI makes data-driven decision-making an integral part of future media relations. By utilizing big data and machine learning, museum PR professionals can better understand audience behaviors, media preferences, and engagement patterns. Such insights facilitate effective campaign planning, message customization, and performance measurement. AI can analyze extensive datasets to determine the best channels and timings for content distribution, ensuring that messages reach the intended audience when most impactful. This newfound level of precision and efficiency is reshaping capabilities within museum PR.

Social media’s continued growth and digital platform influence further mold the future of museum media relations. Social media has revolutionized news consumption and brand interaction, presenting museums with new engagement opportunities. Platforms like YouTube, X (formerly Twitter), Instagram, and Facebook allow museums to share their narratives, respond to public inquiries, and build community relationships, underpinning the need for agility and adaptability in real-time interactions.

reputation managementAI assistanceinfluencersrole in museum prartificial intelligence (AI)role in future media relationsartificial intelligence (AI)predictive analyticsartificial intelligence (AI)data analysis and media monitoringartificial intelligence (AI)content creationInfluencer marketing will keep playing a significant role in shaping museum media relations. Influencers with large, engaged audiences become essential partners in reaching new museum visitors and bolstering credibility. While mega-influencers cast a wide net, micro-influencers often achieve higher engagement through authentic, niche connections. Museums must navigate this evolving landscape by aligning partnerships with influencers whose values and audience resonate with their institutional ethos, ensuring relevance and resonance.

Furthermore, the rise of multimedia content will redefine museum media strategies. Audiences increasingly favor content through videos, podcasts, and interactive media. Museums must adapt by embracing these formats, especially video content, which allows museums to tell compelling stories and engage audiences effectively. Technologies like live streaming, virtual reality (VR), and AR provide immersive experiences that capture attention and deepen engagement with museum content, making them vital components of future communication strategies.

Museums must emphasize transparency and authenticity to gain and maintain public trust as audiences seek reliable information amid information overload and skepticism. PR strategies should prioritize honest communications, ensuring that messages align with brand identity and ethical standards while addressing issues promptly. This authenticity fosters deeper relationships with museum stakeholders and long-term audience engagement.

As the media environment evolves, so too will the role of museum PR professionals. Practitioners must become increasingly versatile, technologically adept, and data-literate to navigate the digital landscape effectively. Skills in data analysis, AI tools, and multimedia content creation are becoming essential. Strategic thinking and creativity will still be vital, helping museums develop campaigns that resonate and capture attention amid the digital din.

Finally, integrated communication strategies will become crucial in museum media relations, as PR, marketing, and advertising converge. Museums must craft comprehensive approaches that align PR efforts with marketing and business objectives, ensuring message coherence across all platforms. Integrated strategies will help museums create unified brand narratives, enhance messaging impact, and deliver measurable results. In summary, the future of media relations in the museum sector promises to be an era influencersauthenticity and alignmentartificial intelligence (AI)efficiency in messagingartificial intelligence (AI)content creationartificial intelligence (AI)application in PRof integration, innovation, and strategic communication, driving more meaningful audience connections and enhancing institutional presence.

info.title: The Role of AI in PR

section.para: The integration of AI into PR practices represents both a promising evolution and a challenging transition for organizations, including museums. AI offers numerous advantages that can significantly enhance the efficiency and efficacy of PR strategies, yet it also introduces a set of complexities and potential drawbacks that need careful consideration.

One of the primary benefits of AI in PR is its ability to enhance data analysis and media monitoring capabilities. For museums, which often interact with a diverse audience through various media channels, AI can sort through vast amounts of data to track mentions, analyze sentiment, and identify trends. This capability allows museum PR teams to quickly respond to public sentiment, tailor their communication strategies more effectively, and anticipate potential challenges before they escalate. For instance, AI can help identify emerging interests in certain exhibits, enabling museums to amplify their marketing efforts targeted at these interests and attract more visitors.

Another major advantage is the efficiency AI brings to content creation and distribution. AI tools can assist in drafting press releases, generating social media posts, and even crafting tailored messages for different audience segments. This can be particularly beneficial for museums with limited resources dedicated to PR, as it allows them to maintain a consistent and engaging online presence without heavily burdening their staff. Additionally, AI-driven tools can optimize the timing and placement of content across digital platforms, ensuring that museum announcements and stories reach the right audience at the right time.

Furthermore, AI’s predictive analytics capabilities empower museums to make data-driven decisions regarding audience engagement and marketing strategies. By analyzing patterns and predicting future trends, museums can align their exhibits and programs with audience preferences, enhancing visitor satisfaction and increasing foot traffic. This proactive approach allows museums to remain relevant and competitive in an ever-evolving cultural landscape.

social media strategyprivacy and security concernssocial mediaprivacy and securityreputation managementPR ethical challengesartificial intelligence (AI)privacy and data securityartificial intelligence (AI)ethical concernsHowever, the use of AI in PR is not without its challenges. One significant con is the potential loss of the human touch in communications. AI systems, while efficient, lack the nuance and empathy that human communication inherently possesses. For museums, which often aim to evoke emotional connections through their exhibits and storytelling, relying too heavily on AI-generated content could result in interactions that feel impersonal or detached from the visitor experience.

Moreover, the implementation of AI technologies can be cost-intensive, particularly for smaller museums with limited budgets. The initial investment in AI tools, along with the ongoing updates and maintenance required, may pose financial challenges. Additionally, the complexity of integrating AI into existing PR practices can necessitate extensive training for staff, adding to the resource demands of the organization.

Another risk associated with AI in PR is data security and privacy concerns. Museums often handle sensitive information regarding donors, members, and research subjects. The use of AI requires robust data protection measures to ensure this information is kept secure from breaches and that compliance with privacy regulations is maintained. Mismanagement of data could lead to significant reputational damage and loss of public trust.

Finally, ethical considerations around AI’s role in PR should not be overlooked. The reliance on algorithms to drive communication strategies may inadvertently perpetuate biases or lead to a homogenization of messages, which can limit the diversity of voices and perspectives represented. Museums must approach AI implementation thoughtfully, ensuring that it augments rather than overrides the rich, varied human insights that form the foundation of effective storytelling and audience engagement.

info.title: Ethical Issues Facing the PR Field

section.para: PR is a field that inherently deals with the management of information and the shaping of public perception, making it susceptible to various ethical issues. As the landscape of PR continues to evolve with technological advancements and changing societal norms, several ethical challenges have emerged and are likely to persist in the future. Addressing these issues is crucial for maintaining the integrity and credibility of the profession.

media relationsrole of PR professionalsOne of the most pressing ethical issues in PR today is the spread of misinformation and disinformation. With the rise of digital media and social platforms, the dissemination of false or misleading information has become alarmingly easy. PR professionals have a responsibility to ensure that the information they share is accurate and truthful. However, the pressure to achieve quick results and the competitive nature of the industry can sometimes lead to the temptation to manipulate facts or omit critical details. This not only undermines public trust but also poses significant risks to the reputation of the organizations involved. Moving forward, PR practitioners must prioritize transparency and accuracy, adhering to ethical standards that promote honesty and integrity in all communications.

Another significant ethical concern is the practice of astroturfing, where organizations create fake grassroots movements to sway public opinion. This deceptive tactic involves the use of paid actors or fake accounts to simulate genuine public support or opposition. Astroturfing erodes trust in authentic grassroots movements and can lead to public cynicism toward genuine advocacy efforts. As digital tools and social media platforms become more sophisticated, the potential for astroturfing increases. PR professionals must resist the temptation to engage in such practices and instead focus on fostering genuine engagement and dialogue with stakeholders.

The issue of privacy and data protection is also a growing ethical challenge in the PR industry. With the increasing reliance on data analytics to inform PR strategies, there is a heightened risk of violating individuals’ privacy rights. Collecting, storing, and using personal data without proper consent or transparency can lead to significant ethical breaches. PR professionals must navigate the fine line between leveraging data for effective communication and respecting the privacy of individuals. Adhering to data protection regulations, such as the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), and implementing robust data security measures are essential steps in addressing this ethical concern.

The rise of influencer marketing has introduced new ethical dilemmas in PR. Influencers, with their large and engaged followings, have become powerful voices in shaping public opinion. However, the lack of transparency in influencer partnerships can lead to ethical issues. For instance, when influencers fail to disclose paid promotions or sponsored content, it can mislead their audience and undermine trust. PR professionals must ensure that all influencer collaborations are transparent and that influencers adhere to disclosure guidelines. This not only protects the integrity of the campaign but also fosters trust between the influencer, the brand, and the audience.

Conflicts of interest represent another ethical challenge in the PR industry. PR professionals often work with multiple clients, and there can be situations where the interests of different clients conflict. Navigating these conflicts requires a high level of ethical judgment and transparency. PR practitioners must disclose any potential conflicts of interest to their clients and take steps to manage them effectively. This may involve recusing themselves from certain projects or ensuring that separate teams handle conflicting accounts to maintain objectivity and fairness.

The ethical use of AI and automation in PR is an emerging concern. While AI offers numerous benefits, such as enhanced data analysis and personalized communication, it also raises ethical questions. For example, the use of AI-generated content or chatbots can blur the lines between human and automated interactions, potentially deceiving the audience. Additionally, biases in AI algorithms can lead to unfair or discriminatory outcomes. PR professionals must ensure that AI tools are used ethically, with transparency about their use and measures in place to mitigate biases.

Lastly, the pressure to achieve immediate results and the emphasis on metrics and performance can sometimes lead to unethical behavior in PR. The focus on short-term gains can drive PR professionals to engage in practices that compromise ethical standards, such as exaggerating results or manipulating metrics. It is essential for the PR industry to foster a culture that values long-term relationships and ethical conduct over short-term achievements. This involves setting realistic expectations with clients and stakeholders and prioritizing ethical considerations in all decision-making processes.

info.title: The Role of PR in Museums

section.para: As the PR landscape evolves with technological advances and shifting societal expectations, the role of the PR professional as a counselor becomes increasingly vital. In the future, PR practitioners will not merely serve as communicators or media liaisons; they will take on the mantle of strategic advisers, guiding organizations through complex landscapes of public perception, reputation management, and ethical communication. This digital mediadigital transformation’s impact on museum PRexpanded role is crucial as organizations, including museums, navigate an era characterized by rapid information flow and heightened public scrutiny.

PR professionals as counselors play a pivotal role in shaping an organization’s strategic direction and ensuring its communications align with broader objectives. Their insights into media trends, audience behaviors, and sociopolitical factors equip them to offer informed advice that supports decision-making at the highest levels. For instance, museums seeking to position themselves as leaders in cultural dialogue will rely on PR counselors to craft narratives that resonate authentically with diverse communities, fostering inclusive engagement while highlighting the institution’s mission and values.

Moreover, PR counselors are instrumental in risk assessment and crisis management. By anticipating potential challenges and crafting preemptive strategies, they help organizations mitigate the impact of crises and maintain public trust. In a museum context, PR professionals can advise on sensitive issues related to exhibit content, ethical acquisitions, or contentious public reactions, ensuring that institutional responses are both proactive and principled.

The counselor role also extends to reputation management and brand stewardship. As organizations face increasing demands for transparency and accountability, PR professionals provide guidance on building and sustaining trust. They help craft messages that reinforce organizational integrity, ensuring that actions and communications reflect consistent values. Museums, in particular, can benefit from PR professionals who counsel on authenticity in storytelling, community relations, and digital engagement strategies, maintaining a coherent narrative across all touchpoints.

In addition, PR counselors serve as ethical guardians within their organizations, ensuring that communications adhere to principles of honesty, respect, and inclusivity. As organizations navigate complex issues ranging from diversity and inclusion to environmental sustainability, PR professionals advocate for ethical considerations in organizational narratives and strategic decisions. This role is especially pertinent for museums, which must grapple with representing diverse histories and cultures responsibly and sensitively.

Finally, PR counselors play a crucial role in fostering innovation and adaptability. Their awareness of emerging trends and technologies enables them to advise organizations on new platforms and strategies for engagement, ensuring that communications remain relevant and effective in a rapidly changing world. For museums, this might involve adopting cutting-edge digital tools for virtual exhibits or leveraging social media analytics to refine audience targeting.

Overall, as the role of the PR professional as a counselor continues to evolve, their strategic insight and ethical guidance will become indispensable assets to organizations. By offering nuanced, forward-thinking advice that spans communication, reputation, and ethical dimensions, PR counselors will help steer institutions like museums through the complexities of modern PR, ensuring their ongoing relevance and resonance with the public.

In today’s fast-paced and digitally interconnected world, internal employee communication within museums has become more critical than ever. The evolving landscape of the museum field, characterized by rapid technological advancements, shifts in audience expectations, and a pressing need for transparency, demands effective communication strategies that align staff across all levels of the organization. The importance of internal communications has been further underscored by the challenges brought about by the Covid-19 pandemic, which has forced museums to adapt to remote and hybrid work models, pushing the need for clear, consistent, and comprehensive communication to the forefront of operational priorities.

Museums, traditionally seen as bastions of culture and education, are increasingly called upon to engage with global audiences while catering to diverse local communities. This dual responsibility requires adept internal communication to ensure that all staff—ranging from curators and administrators to educators and technical support—are on the same page and working toward unified goals. In this context, effective communication serves as the backbone for museums to fulfill their missions successfully. It ensures that every department understands its role in advancing the museum’s objectives, thereby promoting coherence and collaboration across the board.

One of the fundamental reasons why internal communication is so crucial today is the ongoing digital transformation. As museums incorporate more digital interactions into their offerings, whether through virtual exhibitions or interactive online content, the complexity of operations increases. This transformation requires seamless communication among staff to ensure new technologies are integrated smoothly and effectively. Moreover, with the pandemic having accelerated the adoption of digital tools, many museum staff are now working in hybrid environments, making robust internal communication systems essential for maintaining productivity and engagement.

The diverse nature of museum audiences demands that museums cultivate cultural competency and inclusiveness within their staff. Effective internal communication fosters an organizational culture that values diversity, equity, and inclusion, equipping employees to develop programs and exhibits that resonate with a broad spectrum of visitors. As museums strive to reflect the diversity of their communities, internal communication plays a critical role in ensuring that staff are aware of and sensitive to cultural nuances and are able to incorporate these into their work.

The growing scrutiny of public institutions, including museums, necessitates transparency and ethical practices. In this environment, museums are under constant observation to maintain credibility and public trust. Internal communication is vital in keeping staff informed about institutional values, ethical standards, and crisis management strategies. This ensures that all employees are prepared to represent the museum appropriately, safeguard its reputation, and respond effectively to external challenges.

Effective internal communication is not only about addressing challenges but also about enhancing the museum’s internal environment. For instance, clear communication enhances employee engagement and morale by helping staff understand how their work fits into the museum’s larger mission. Particularly in museums, where resources can be scarce and roles multifaceted, knowing that one’s work is contributing to a greater purpose can significantly boost motivation and satisfaction.

To be successful in internal communications, museums must implement several key strategies. First, establishing clear and consistent communication channels is essential. Museums can rely on a combination of intranets, newsletters, team meetings, and digital collaboration tools to relay information effectively. Regular updates about museum activities, upcoming events, and strategic initiatives keep staff informed and engaged. Encouraging open dialogue and feedback is equally important. Creating a culture where staff feel comfortable sharing their thoughts and concerns fosters trust and transparency. Museums can facilitate this by holding town hall meetings, conducting surveys, and having feedback sessions. At the Natural History Museum in London, for example, staff input was actively solicited during renovation projects, ensuring buy-in and reducing resistance to change.

Investment in training and development also plays a crucial role in fostering effective communication. By offering workshops on communication skills, leadership, and cultural competency, museums can empower staff to communicate more effectively across departments. For example, the Field Museum in Chicago provides ongoing professional development opportunities, enhancing both individual capabilities and overall organizational communication. Leveraging technology to facilitate communication is another strategy that museums can benefit from. Digital platforms such as social media, instant messaging, and collaboration tools improve real-time communication and information sharing. The British Museum, for instance, uses digital tools to connect its global staff network, ensuring seamless communication across different time zones while promoting a cohesive organizational culture.

Recognizing and rewarding effective communication within the organization reinforces its importance and encourages a culture of openness and mutual respect. Museums can implement recognition programs to highlight employees who contribute significantly to successful communication initiatives, thus motivating others to engage actively in internal communications.

Moreover, internal communications play a pivotal role in crisis situations, ensuring that staff are well-informed and prepared to act. Whether managing PR challenges or handling natural disasters, having a comprehensive internal communication plan in place enables museums to respond swiftly and cohesively. For example, The J. Paul Getty Museum in California has a well-established emergency communication plan, ensuring all staff are aware of their responsibilities during crises, minimizing confusion, and enhancing the institution’s resilience.

Interview with Mike Bova, senior vice president at Dezenhall Resources, and David Fuscus, president and CEO, Xenophon Strategies. As a senior vice ask the expertMike Bovaask the expertDavid Fuscuspresident at Dezenhall Resources, Mike Bova specializes in complex crisis management, media relations, and the development of impactful public affairs campaigns for client issues. Bova also serves as a strategic adviser to numerous clients dealing with complex litigation and legislation.

David A. Fuscus is CEO and president of Xenophon Strategies, a highly focused PR firm serving many of the world’s largest companies and organizations. Founded in 2000, Xenophon has key practices in public affairs, PR, reputation management, crisis communications, and government affairs. Xenophon represents clients from the United States, Canada, Europe, Asia, and Central Asia.

para.emphasis: Q: As a society, we’ve lost a lot of trust in the media. Do you think it will get better in the future? What needs to change?

section.para: Mike Bova: That is a fairly loaded question, but I am hopeful that we will slowly begin to trust our institutions more; however, that trust has to be earned. Media organizations will need to commit to holding themselves to higher journalistic standards that have been lowered due to chasing clicks, ratings, and always having to always be first. Many of my clients are being asked to comment on issues that, a decade ago, I did not believe to be newsworthy or worth reporting on at all. Regardless, I am hopeful that as we see a shift toward subscription models, media institutions will regain the public’s trust while also having the resources to produce a good product.

David Fuscus: The current crisis in media trust isn’t just a temporary problem—it’s a fundamental challenge to how we communicate as a society. Traditional media has lost significant credibility, driven by a perfect storm of 24/7 news cycles, social media echo chambers, and financial pressures pushing quantity over quality. However, there’s room for optimism. Three key developments suggest possible improvement: increasing transparency in newsrooms, a budding revival of local journalism, and a growing emphasis on media literacy education. These changes are crucial stepping stones toward rebuilding public trust.

Moving forward, success depends on news organizations finding the right balance between maintaining rigorous journalistic standards and adapting to modern communication needs. While we won’t see an overnight transformation, gradual improvement is possible if media outlets prioritize credibility and public service over speed and sensationalism. The solution isn’t about returning to the past, but rather creating a new model of trust built on transparency, accountability, and verified facts. It’s a long road ahead, but the foundation for recovery is being laid.

Q. Surveys show that museums are trusted institutions, but the media is not trusted. Why should museums even pursue earned media? Mike Bova: I would push back on the premise that all media is not trusted. I think it is certainly fragmented, but everyone has their own source of information on any given topic and current events. Opting out entirely of trying to leverage the reach of news sources will hinder any organization’s ability to reach key audiences. It also depends on the type of information and the story you are pitching. Local media remains a trusted source of community events; a museum can leverage this. These types of publications are also eager to engage with organizations that have this type of news to share because it is hyper-local, relevant, and informative for their audience.

Museums likely have more to say than the media has the capacity to cover, or you may wish to communicate on certain topics in a way that requires perfect message control. It’s crucial that any messenger evaluates the different media and tools available to reach its stakeholders effectively and then make a decision. I do, however, believe there is a growing role for the use of owned properties (websites, blogs, social channels, podcasts, and Substacks) that organizations like museums can create themselves and use their well-earned bank of trust to reach specific audiences.

David Fuscus: Pursuing earned media is crucial for public-facing institutions like museums, despite the current distrust in media. Earned media serves as a powerful platform to amplify their voice, share stories, and promote educational programs to reach a wider audience than just the museum community. When trusted institutions like museums are featured in the media, it enhances credibility for both the museum and the media outlet. Additionally, earned media increases visibility for unique exhibitions and events, drawing more visitors and participants.

Engaging with media also allows museums to convey their values and address important social issues, helping to position them as thought leaders within their communities. Furthermore, media coverage can spark public interest and dialogue, fostering deeper relationships with audiences. Ultimately, while trust in media may be waning, museums can leverage earned media to strengthen their missions, enhance community engagement, and reinforce public trust.

para.emphasis: Q. In the future, should I skip pitching news outlets altogether and go directly to our visitors or donors?

section.para: Mike Bova: There should be a healthy balance of the two. Going directly to visitors and donors is the best way to control your message, but you are limiting your reach to those that already support your organization or have already visited. Earned media allows you to reach a new audience and hopefully convert them into donors and visitors that can then be targeted with your owned content. Additionally, while the credibility of news outlets continues to wane, there is a benefit to having an external third-party validator tell an audience your news; it comes off as less of a sales pitch and more of a news event worth paying attention to.

The challenge for many organizations today is not to get sucked into any unwanted cultural discussion that is not directly relevant to what they are trying to communicate. As I have seen working in the crisis management discipline, there are always motivated adversaries waiting to pounce on any side comment made or trying to lure you into a culture war unnecessarily.

David Fuscus: Museums should not choose between earned media and direct outreach to visitors or donors; rather, both are essential components of a comprehensive PR strategy. Earned media is crucial for amplifying your message and increasing visibility, lending credibility to the museum, and attracting new audiences. However, direct outreach is equally important for fostering relationships with visitors and donors. Personalized communications and newsletters can transform passive audience members into engaged supporters, creating a sense of community around your museum.

Additionally, a strong social media strategy focused on visual platforms like Instagram, TikTok, and Reels is crucial for reaching younger audiences. Engaging content, such as behind-the-scenes tours or educational snippets, can enhance a museum’s relevance and immediacy. Participating in community events and collaborations strengthens a museum’s brand presence, while initiatives like “Ask a Curator” days can invite the public to get involved. Exploring partnerships with local influencers can also broaden an institution’s reach.

A successful PR approach for museums involves a balanced integration of earned media, direct outreach, social media engagement, and community involvement and helps to create a vibrant and supportive relationship with the public.

para.emphasis: Q. What is the future of social media? Is that still an effective channel to reach target audiences?

section.para: Mike Bova: I think you can likely write another book on the question of what the future of social media holds. Yes, social media is still an effective channel to reach target audiences. Whether we like it or not, just over half of US adults (54 percent) say they at least sometimes get news from social media, according to a recent Pew Research survey, and that number continues to grow each year. Not all social media is created equal; it’s important for organizations to use the channels and create the types of content that best suit their audiences.

David Fuscus: The future of social media will be dynamic and continue to be essential for reaching audiences. With over 5 billion users globally, social media’s influence is set to grow, especially among those engaging with multiple platforms. Users increasingly prefer niche communities and smaller platforms, driven by a desire for authenticity and meaningful connections.

Visual storytelling will play a pivotal role in this future as platforms like TikTok and Instagram Reels rise in popularity. Engaging, entertaining content will be crucial for capturing audience attention. Additionally, social media advertising remains highly effective; nearly 49 percent of internet users are likely to purchase from brands they discover through social media ads. This emphasizes the value of targeted strategies and partnerships with micro-influencers to build trust and enhance engagement.

Ultimately, adaptability is key as brands navigate this evolving landscape. By embracing new platforms, optimizing content for search, and ensuring responsive customer service, organizations can effectively connect with and engage their audiences. Social media is not just an effective channel—it’s a critical one for future communication and brand growth.

para.emphasis: Q. What is the best use of AI in public relations? Can it be used for museums public relations, especially small museums that don’t have a PR department?

section.para: Mike Bova: The advancements in AI that have taken place in such a short amount of time have been fascinating. The productivity and innovation gains that will result will be massive. From a communications standpoint, a lot of the application has been preliminary research assistance and the first iteration of materials—vastly reducing the time spent to collect and sort information and data. Both of those applications are a starting point; they do not replace the entire process, and for good reason. As they stand right now, the AI technologies available to us are not accurate enough or advanced enough to wholeheartedly trust. However, they can save time, give you somewhere to start, and use your expertise to help shape whatever materials you are working on more efficiently.

If we intend to incorporate this powerful technology into our daily operations, we must do so responsibly, ensuring that it enhances rather than replaces our human talent and expertise. Persuasion’s true power lies in its subtlety and nuance—no one-size-fits-all message or approach exists. While technological advancements have allowed us to communicate more authentically by leveraging data and targeting, our success stems from strategic thinking that encompasses consumer values, emotional connections, and historical perspectives. We excel because we understand the complexity of human nature—a quality that large learning models cannot replicate. Embracing human irrationality—the stuff that makes life interesting—becomes vital because the individuals we aim to engage with do not see the world as a series of 1s and 0s.

At my firm, Dezenhall, we stand at the crossroads of excitement and curiosity regarding AI’s impact. We are early adopters of innovative technologies, constantly exploring new tools and techniques that could enhance our work and drive successful outcomes for our clients. However, we are also skeptical of AI’s eventual power to replace our experts. If AI becomes a tool to empower human intellect, it will move society forward. If it becomes a vehicle to replace humanity with the lowest common denominator “thinking,” we are much less excited.

David Fuscus: Generative AI (GAI) hasn’t been around all that long, ChatGPT was only launched in late 2022. Generalist GAI tools like ChatGPT are useful, but they are built to be all things to all people and can often take a great deal of work to get to a quality end product. Specialist AI tools are just beginning to appear on the market, and our product, Précis Public Relations, is the first and leading PR AI product focused primarily on content production, it is an everyday AI assistant. Industry-specific AI platforms like Précis are designed for public-facing communications and offer an effective solution for small museums without dedicated PR departments.

And generative AI offers dramatic productivity gains and access to advanced PR skills that small companies and organizations need. For example, Précis users report big time savings that reduce PR task completion time by 50-70 percent, which would allow museums to maintain professional PR programs despite limited staff and resources. For small museums seeking to enhance their PR capabilities, purpose-built communications AI platforms represent a cost-effective way to maintain professional, engaging outreach programs that might otherwise be beyond their reach.

para.emphasis: Q. Regarding of the size of a museum, how important is internal employee communications?

section.para: Mike Bova: Internal communications, including HR policies, are often the most overlooked tactics in a communicator’s toolbox, yet they are more important than ever. This channel allows you to highlight inspiring stories within your organization while directly engaging your team, bypassing traditional media, and controlling the context in which your message is delivered. This forum lets you gently introduce traditionally controversial issues, fostering more dialogue than a sermon. By embodying your values rather than merely stating them, organizations can credibly demonstrate to those closest to them that certain progressive policies are true priorities for the company.

Do not be tempted to take this to an extreme and get over your skis—focus on equality of opportunity, safe spaces for all employees, and making your company a place where a diverse group of people all feel seen, protected, and empowered, this can pay dividends toward your reputational enterprise value. This can be done in a controlled, reasonable environment that keeps you off the bad side of the trending social media pages while giving brand stewards real, credible feedback on where to listen and learn and, most importantly, when it is the right time to take a stand.

chapter.para: Steven E. Lott is a corporate communications executive with more than twenty years of experience developing strategic public relations (PR) strategies and brand campaigns across diverse industries including aerospace, manufacturing, transportation, consumer brands, and international trade policy. He is also a professor of strategic communication at American University (AU), where he teaches a graduate-level university course about media relations.

Lott started his career as a journalist, learning how to research, write, and tell captivating stories to a wide variety of audiences. Now a corporate communications executive, Lott brings decades of real-world experience to many different industries. Whether he’s working with corporate executives, nonprofit leaders, or students, Lott trains leaders without any experience to develop captivating stories and earn news media coverage that will reach their target audience. Using proven PR strategies and tactics, Lott regularly consults, provides spokesperson training, and teaches crisis communication strategies and how to deal with organizational reputational damage.

Lott currently leads global corporate communications and PR for SES (formerly Intelsat), one of the world’s largest integrated satellite and terrestrial network operators. Previously, he served as a corporate communications executive at RTX and Boeing. Before joining Boeing, Lott worked at two different nonprofit trade associations and was a journalist with the Aviation Week Network.

Lott is currently an adjunct professor in the AU School of Communication and is an adviser to the Northern Virginia Science Center on communication matters. Lott graduated from AU’s Kogod College of Business with degrees in marketing and business administration.
